questions.explain: Clue: "swung wildly" and "absorb shocks." Signal: "Because" (cause) and "skepticism ... few believed" (doubt). Predict: (i) steady, (ii) small. Stabilize fits a promise aimed at wild swings; meager explains the doubt. Trap: ample would make the stock adequate and undercut "skepticism." Volatile describes the price, not the size of a reserve. Liberalize and inflate do not answer wild swings. Words: stabilize = make steady; liberalize = remove controls; meager = inadequate in amount; ample = more than enough; volatile = liable to sudden change. Lesson: "skepticism" and "few believed" call for a word that makes the plan look inadequate.

questions.stem: The ambassador's reputation for (i)_____ was well earned: in thirty years of negotiation she never once made a promise she could not keep or a threat she did not mean, a record that made her counterparts (ii)_____ to call her bluffs.
questions.explain: Clue: "never once made a promise she could not keep or a threat she did not mean." Signal: colon (explanation) and "a record that made" (consequence). Predict: (i) honesty, (ii) unwilling. Probity and loath fit: if her threats are always real, calling a "bluff" is dangerous. Trap: duplicity is the opposite-direction word (deceit); bluster suggests empty threats. Eager reverses the consequence. Words: probity = strict honesty, integrity; duplicity = deceitfulness; bluster = loud empty talk; loath = reluctant. Lesson: work out the consequence step by step: real threats mean no one dares to test them.

questions.stem: Much early scholarship treated the city's immigrant enclaves as way stations whose residents would soon (i)_____ into the wider society; yet many enclaves persisted for generations, suggesting that they served less as transit points than as (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "way stations," "persisted for generations," "less as transit points than as." Signal: "yet" (contrast). Predict: (i) blend in, (ii) lasting homes. Assimilate and enduring communities fit. Trap: temporary refuges and points of departure both restate "way stations" and "transit points," the view the sentence rejects. Withdraw and secede move away from the wider society, the wrong direction for a way station. Words: enclave = a distinct group within a larger territory; assimilate = become absorbed into a culture; secede = formally withdraw. Lesson: "less as X than as" means the answer must contrast with X; reject options that are X in other words.

questions.stem: The critic's early reviews were so uniformly (i)_____ that publishers came to dread them; later, when he began to praise a few writers, the very rarity of his approval made it (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "publishers came to dread them"; "rarity of his approval." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence) and "later" (contrast in time). Predict: (i) harsh, (ii) highly valued. Scathing and coveted fit: what is rare is prized. Trap: laudatory is the opposite direction; no one dreads praise. Equivocal reviews would not inspire dread. Worthless and predictable reverse the logic of rarity. Words: scathing = severely critical; laudatory = praising; equivocal = ambiguous; coveted = eagerly desired. Lesson: scarcity creates value; "very rarity ... made it" points to something prized.

questions.stem: The museum's new wing, intended to (i)_____ the original building's neoclassical facade, instead overwhelms it; its glass bulk makes the older structure look less like a centerpiece than like (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "intended to ... instead overwhelms it." Signal: "instead" means the intention differs from the result. Predict: (i) enhance, set off, (ii) something minor. Complement and an afterthought fit. Trap: eclipse describes what the wing actually did, so it cannot be the intention; it fits locally but breaks "instead." Replicate fails because glass does not copy neoclassical stone. A culmination and a model are prominent, contradicting "less like a centerpiece." Words: complement = complete, enhance by contrast; eclipse = overshadow; replicate = copy; culmination = highest point. Lesson: "intended ... instead" sets intention against result; the blank sits on the intention side.

questions.stem: Jazz improvisation is sometimes imagined as pure invention, conjured from nothing in the moment. Musicians themselves describe something closer to (i)_____: years of absorbing licks, patterns, and harmonic formulas that, in performance, are recombined so fluidly that the result sounds (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "conjured from nothing" (the myth) vs "years of absorbing ... formulas" (the reality); "recombined so fluidly." Signal: "something closer to" (correction) and "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) memory, (ii) spontaneous. Recollection and extemporaneous fit: stored material is recalled yet sounds improvised. Trap: rehearsed fits "years of absorbing" locally but contradicts "so fluidly"; fluency makes it sound unplanned. Inspiration and revelation restate the "from nothing" myth. Derivative ignores "fluidly." Words: extemporaneous = done without preparation; derivative = unoriginal. Lesson: in "so ... that," the result follows from the specific cause (fluid recombination), not from the general context.

questions.stem: The philosopher hedged every claim with so many qualifications that his critics could find nothing to refute; the price of this (i)_____, however, was that his admirers could find nothing to (ii)_____ either.
questions.explain: Clue: "hedged every claim with so many qualifications"; "nothing to refute" ... "nothing to ___ either." Signal: "the price of this ... however" (a cost) and "either" (parallel). Predict: (i) carefulness, (ii) adopt. Caution and embrace fit: critics have nothing to attack, admirers nothing to hold on to. Trap: dispute repeats "refute," but admirers do not dispute; the parallel needs the admirers' own action. Audacity is the opposite of hedging; clarity is undermined by endless qualification. Words: hedge = qualify to avoid commitment; audacity = boldness; refute = disprove. Lesson: "either" sets up a parallel; match each group with its own natural action.

questions.stem: Economists had long assumed that consumers were (i)_____ calculators who weighed every purchase against its alternatives; experiments showing that the mere order in which options are presented sways choices have made that assumption look (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "weighed every purchase against its alternatives" vs "mere order ... sways choices." Signal: none explicit; "had long assumed" plus contrary evidence implies the assumption is outdated. Predict: (i) logical, (ii) outdated. Rational and quaint fit. Trap: prescient and robust treat the assumption as confirmed, the opposite of what the experiments show. Impulsive and myopic describe the experiments' consumers, not the calculators of the old assumption. Words: myopic = short-sighted; quaint = charmingly old-fashioned, outdated; prescient = foreseeing the future; robust = strong, holding up. Lesson: "had long assumed" usually sets up an assumption about to be undermined.

questions.stem: The constitution's framers left the scope of executive power deliberately (i)_____, trusting that future generations would settle by practice what they could not settle by text; the result has been two centuries of (ii)_____ over precisely those questions.
questions.explain: Clue: "settle by practice what they could not settle by text." Signal: "the result has been" (consequence). Predict: (i) unclear, (ii) dispute. Ambiguous and contention fit: what text leaves open, later generations fight over. Trap: explicit and circumscribed both mean settled by text, the opposite of what the framers did. Consensus contradicts the idea that the questions still had to be settled; indifference contradicts "precisely those questions" being pressing. Words: circumscribed = clearly limited; contention = heated disagreement. Lesson: in a consequence clause, ask what follows from the specific gap the first clause created.

questions.stem: Contrary to the stereotype of the (i)_____ teenager who communicates in monosyllables, the adolescents in the study proved (ii)_____ when asked about subjects that mattered to them, often talking for an hour without prompting.
questions.explain: Clue: "communicates in monosyllables" defines (i); "talking for an hour without prompting" defines (ii). Signal: "Contrary to" (contrast). Predict: (i) silent, (ii) talkative. Taciturn and voluble fit. Trap: garrulous is the opposite-direction pick for (i); it describes the study's teens, not the stereotype. Laconic and reticent are synonyms of taciturn, so they belong to the stereotype, not the finding. Words: taciturn = habitually silent; garrulous = excessively talkative; precocious = advanced for one's age; voluble = speaking fluently and at length; laconic = using few words; reticent = reserved. Lesson: when you know a word pair (taciturn / garrulous), locate each blank's own clue before choosing.

questions.stem: Readers who know the novel only through its film adaptation imagine a (i)_____ romance; the book itself is far darker, its love story merely the pretext for a (ii)_____ dissection of the class system that made such love impossible.
questions.explain: Clue: "the book itself is far darker" (so the film version is light); "dissection of the class system." Signal: semicolon with "far darker" (contrast between film and book). Predict: (i) sweet, (ii) unsparing. Sentimental and merciless fit. Trap: bleak describes the book, not the film, so it breaks the contrast. Satirical is not the opposite of "darker." Genial and cursory contradict "far darker" and "dissection." Words: sentimental = appealing to tender emotions; satirical = mocking; merciless = showing no pity; genial = friendly; cursory = hasty. Lesson: "far darker" tells you the first blank must be light; do not fill it with the book's own quality.

questions.stem: Because the medieval workshop prized fidelity to established models over personal expression, its artists rarely signed their works; so thoroughly was individual style (i)_____ that modern scholars can often assign a panel to a workshop but almost never to (ii)_____ hand.
questions.explain: Clue: "prized fidelity to established models over personal expression"; "rarely signed." Signal: "Because" and "so ... that" (cause and consequence). Predict: (i) suppressed, (ii) individual. Subordinated and particular fit: scholars can name the workshop but not the individual. Trap: anonymous and collective describe what scholars CAN identify (the group), but the sentence contrasts the workshop with a single hand. Celebrated and cultivated are the opposite direction. Words: subordinate = treat as less important; cultivate = develop; particular = specific, individual. Lesson: "assign to X but never to Y" means Y contrasts with X; here workshop vs individual.

questions.stem: The symphony's premiere was a fiasco, the audience jeering through its dissonant final movement; yet within a generation the work had become so (i)_____ a part of the repertoire that its (ii)_____ is now hard to imagine.
questions.explain: Clue: "fiasco," "jeering" vs "within a generation ... part of the repertoire." Signal: "yet" (contrast) and "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) established, (ii) its bad start. Ingrained and early notoriety fit: the work is now so established that its scandalous premiere is hard to picture. Trap: canonical status is the work's present condition, which is easy to imagine, since it is true. Peripheral and precarious contradict becoming a fixture. Technical difficulty is never mentioned. Words: ingrained = firmly fixed, deep-rooted; peripheral = marginal; precarious = unstable; notoriety = fame for something bad; canonical = accepted as a classic. Lesson: "so established that its ___ is hard to imagine" points backward to the past it has outgrown.

questions.stem: Socrates professed (i)_____, insisting that he knew nothing; but his interlocutors often suspected that the profession was (ii)_____, a pose that allowed him to expose their ignorance while concealing his own convictions.
questions.explain: Clue: "insisting that he knew nothing" defines (i); "a pose" and "concealing his own convictions" define (ii). Signal: "but ... suspected" (contrast). Predict: (i) not knowing, (ii) insincere. Ignorance and disingenuous fit. Trap: heartfelt is the opposite direction; "a pose" is not sincere. Incoherent attacks the logic, not the sincerity. Omniscience is the opposite of "knew nothing." Words: profess = claim openly; omniscience = knowing everything; disingenuous = not candid, pretending to know less than one does; incoherent = lacking logical connection. Lesson: an appositive ("a pose that ...") right after a blank is its definition; read it before the choices.

questions.stem: The firm's quarterly report was a masterpiece of (i)_____. Losses appeared as "negative growth," layoffs as "workforce optimization," and a failed product launch as "a learning opportunity." Investors who read past the vocabulary found the company's position (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: losses, layoffs, and failure renamed with soft phrases; investors who "read past the vocabulary." Signal: none explicit; the examples define (i), and "read past" implies a reality different from the wording. Predict: (i) soft-pedaling, (ii) dangerous. Euphemism and parlous fit. Trap: robust accepts the report's spin. Ambiguous fails because the facts beneath (losses, layoffs) are plainly bad. Candor is the opposite-direction word; hyperbole is exaggeration, but these phrases understate. Words: euphemism = a mild term for something unpleasant; candor = frankness; hyperbole = exaggeration; parlous = precarious, dangerous. Lesson: examples are definitions; a list of soft labels defines euphemism, not hyperbole.

questions.stem: The "temporary" emergency powers granted during the war were renewed so routinely in the decades that followed that the adjective eventually became (i)_____; scholars now cite the case as a textbook example of how exceptional measures can become (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "temporary" in quotation marks; "renewed so routinely in the decades." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) no longer accurate, used with irony, (ii) routine. Ironic and normalized fit. Trap: derogatory would mean "temporary" became an insult; it merely stopped being true. Apt is the opposite: decades of renewal make "temporary" inaccurate. Abolished contradicts renewal; exceptional repeats the starting point instead of the change. Words: ironic = meaning the opposite of what is said; apt = fitting; derogatory = disparaging; normalized = made routine. Lesson: a label that stops matching reality becomes ironic (or a misnomer), not an insult.

questions.stem: The sociologist's findings on neighborhood trust were initially greeted as (i)_____, overturning decades of received wisdom; but when other research teams repeatedly failed to reproduce them, enthusiasm gave way to (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "overturning decades of received wisdom"; "failed to reproduce"; "enthusiasm gave way to." Signal: "initially" and "but" (change over time). Predict: (i) groundbreaking, (ii) doubt. Revolutionary and skepticism fit. Trap: spurious fits the LATER verdict, not the initial greeting, so it breaks "initially greeted" and "enthusiasm." Pedestrian contradicts "overturning." Adulation continues the enthusiasm rather than replacing it; complacency does not follow failed replication. Words: pedestrian = dull, ordinary; spurious = false, fake; adulation = excessive praise. Lesson: time markers (initially / later) assign each blank to a moment; fill each with that moment's attitude.

questions.stem: The memoirist is too (i)_____ to flatter herself: where another writer might have cast her younger self as a misunderstood rebel, she presents a girl who was vain, (ii)_____, and frequently cruel, sparing herself none of the judgments she passes on others.
questions.explain: Clue: "too ___ to flatter herself" and "sparing herself none of the judgments." Signal: "too ... to" and a list "vain, ___, and frequently cruel" (continuation of faults). Predict: (i) honest, unsentimental, (ii) a fault. Clear-eyed and petty fit. Trap: vainglorious and indulgent would make her LIKELY to flatter herself, reversing "too ... to." Magnanimous and long-suffering are virtues that break a list of faults. Words: clear-eyed = realistic, unsentimental; vainglorious = boastfully vain; petty = small-minded; magnanimous = generous, forgiving. Lesson: a list in a series takes items of the same polarity; one virtue in a list of faults is a trap.

questions.stem: The forger's skill lay not in (i)_____ any single painting, which would have invited direct comparison, but in producing new works so (ii)_____ of the master's manner that experts assumed they were lost originals.
questions.explain: Clue: "which would have invited direct comparison" and "new works"; "experts assumed they were lost originals." Signal: "not in ... but in" (contrast between two methods). Predict: (i) duplicating, (ii) suggestive of. Copying and redolent fit. Trap: independent sounds like praise for "new works," but works independent of the master's manner would never pass as his. Dismissive does not take "of the master's manner" sensibly. Authenticating is the experts' job, not the forger's. Words: disparage = belittle; redolent of = strongly suggestive of; independent = not influenced by. Lesson: test the consequence: only a word meaning "like the master" leads experts to assume lost originals.

questions.stem: Critics who dismissed the minimalist composers as (i)_____, merely repeating a figure until the listener grew numb, overlooked the subtle (ii)_____ embedded in the repetition: each cycle differs from its predecessor by a single note or beat.
questions.explain: Clue: "merely repeating a figure until the listener grew numb" defines (i); "each cycle differs from its predecessor" defines (ii). Signal: "overlooked" (the critics missed something) and colon (explanation). Predict: (i) repetitive, (ii) change. Monotonous and variation fit. Trap: uniformity and stasis repeat the critics' charge, which "overlooked" says is wrong. Eclectic (drawing on many sources) and bombastic (inflated) do not match "merely repeating." Words: monotonous = tediously unvarying; eclectic = drawing from diverse sources; bombastic = pompous; stasis = inactivity, no change. Lesson: after "overlooked," the blank names what the critics missed, so it contradicts their view.

questions.stem: Pascal's wager does not attempt to prove that God exists. It argues instead that belief is the prudent bet given our uncertainty. Its force, then, is (i)_____ rather than evidential, and objections that it fails to supply (ii)_____ for God's existence miss its aim.
questions.explain: Clue: "does not attempt to prove" and "the prudent bet given our uncertainty." Signal: "then" (conclusion) and "rather than evidential" (contrast). Predict: (i) practical, (ii) evidence. Pragmatic and proof fit: the wager is about what is wise to do, so objecting that it lacks proof misses its aim. Trap: incentive is exactly what the wager DOES supply, so objecting that it lacks one would not miss its aim. Empirical is a kind of evidential reasoning, so it cannot contrast with "evidential." Theological names the topic, not the type of force. Words: pragmatic = concerned with practical consequences; empirical = based on observation. Lesson: "X rather than Y" requires X to be a genuine alternative to Y, not a version of it.

questions.stem: Critics of the merger warned that the combined firm would wield (i)_____ power, free to raise prices without fear of losing customers; regulators, however, found the market still so (ii)_____ that any attempt to do so would simply send buyers to rival suppliers.
questions.explain: Clue: "free to raise prices without fear of losing customers" defines (i); "send buyers to rival suppliers" defines (ii). Signal: "however" (contrast) and "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) dominant over the market, (ii) full of rivals. Monopolistic and competitive fit. Trap: concentrated supports the critics' worry, the opposite of what "however" requires. Stagnant does not explain why buyers can switch. Negligible contradicts "free to raise prices"; fiduciary refers to trust duties, not market power. Words: monopolistic = controlling a market alone; fiduciary = involving a duty held in trust; concentrated (market) = dominated by few firms. Lesson: "however" flips the critics' claim; pick the market condition that defeats it.

questions.stem: The revolutionary leader's speeches were (i)_____, promising a complete break with the past; his conduct in office was strikingly (ii)_____, retaining most of the old regime's ministries, laws, and officials.
questions.explain: Clue: "promising a complete break with the past" defines (i); "retaining most of the old regime's ministries, laws, and officials" defines (ii). Signal: none explicit; "strikingly" and the content imply a contrast between words and deeds. Predict: (i) fiery, (ii) cautious, preserving. Incendiary and conservative fit. Trap: radical matches the speeches, not the conduct, and contradicts "retaining." Erratic implies inconsistency, but his conduct consistently preserved the old order. Conciliatory and tepid are the opposite of "complete break." Words: incendiary = inflammatory; conciliatory = intended to placate; tepid = lukewarm; conservative = favoring the existing order. Lesson: when no signal word appears, compare the two definitions; opposed content means opposed words.

questions.stem: Once a marker of genuine distinction, the honorary degree was conferred so indiscriminately (on donors, celebrities, and local officials alike) that it lost its (i)_____; by the century's end, recipients who listed it on their résumés risked appearing (ii)_____ rather than distinguished.
questions.explain: Clue: "marker of genuine distinction" and "conferred so indiscriminately." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence) and "rather than distinguished" (contrast). Predict: (i) prestige, (ii) showing off. Cachet and pretentious fit: flaunting a cheapened honor looks like pretending. Trap: eminent means distinguished, which the sentence rules out. Modest contradicts listing it on a résumé. Ubiquity and triviality are what the degree GAINED, not what it lost. Words: cachet = prestige; ubiquity = being everywhere; pretentious = claiming more importance than is warranted; eminent = famous, respected. Lesson: "lost its ___" needs a quality it had before; check which state the blank belongs to.

questions.stem: The scholar's edition is (i)_____ in its textual apparatus, recording every variant reading across a dozen manuscripts, yet (ii)_____ in its interpretive notes, which seldom venture beyond a line or two.
questions.explain: Clue: "recording every variant reading" defines (i); "seldom venture beyond a line or two" defines (ii). Signal: "yet" (contrast between the two parts). Predict: (i) complete, (ii) brief, economical. Painstaking and sparing fit. Trap: prolix is the opposite-direction word for (ii), meaning wordy; it would match blank (i)'s abundance, not the brevity described. Sketchy contradicts "every variant." Tendentious and dogmatic concern bias, not quantity. Words: painstaking = extremely thorough; textual apparatus = the record of variants in a scholarly edition; tendentious = promoting a particular view; sparing = economical, restrained; prolix = tediously long. Lesson: when each blank has its own definition, solve each against its own clue, then check that "yet" contrasts them.

questions.stem: Although the historian's new survey of the Mughal court is hardly (i)_____ (she admits in her preface that whole provinces receive no more than a paragraph), her treatment of the topics she does take up is remarkably (ii)_____. Readers seeking a complete account will be disappointed, but those willing to accept her (iii)_____ approach will find few guides more penetrating.
questions.explain: Clues: 'whole provinces receive no more than a paragraph' and 'Readers seeking a complete account will be disappointed' tell you what she is NOT; 'few guides more penetrating' tells you what she IS. Predict (i) complete, (ii) sharp, (iii) limited in scope. Exhaustive, incisive, selective agree with each other and with both clues. Trap: cursory in (ii) echoes 'a paragraph' locally, but 'Although... hardly' sets (ii) against (i), and 'penetrating' demands praise. Encyclopedic in (iii) contradicts blank (i) and the 'complete account' sentence. Lucid in (i) is unrelated to coverage. Definitions: incisive = sharply analytical; cursory = hasty, superficial; diffuse = spread out, unfocused; partisan = biased; polemical = aggressively argumentative. Lesson: decide what the text says the work lacks before you fill in what it has; the two must not overlap.

questions.stem: The director's admirers call her style (i)_____, but this is to mistake a limitation for a virtue: what looks like restraint is often simply a failure of nerve. Her camera rarely moves, her actors rarely raise their voices, and the result, scene after scene, is less (ii)_____ than (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'what looks like restraint' is what admirers see, so (i) is a flattering word for restraint: austere. 'Mistake a limitation for a virtue' fixes the order of (ii) and (iii): 'less VIRTUE than LIMITATION.' So (ii) disciplined, (iii) inert. Trap: lethargic in (ii) plus taut in (iii) reverses the critic's verdict (less sluggish than tight is praise), though each word sits comfortably next to 'camera rarely moves.' Flamboyant contradicts 'restraint'; garish and ornate are about showiness, the opposite of this style. Definitions: austere = severe, unadorned; inert = lifeless, motionless; taut = tight, tense; garish = gaudy; derivative = imitative. Lesson: in 'less X than Y', X is the label the writer rejects; match it to the view the writer opposes.

questions.stem: Economists long treated the informal sector of developing economies as a (i)_____ phenomenon, a transitional holdover destined to disappear as modern industry expanded. Its stubborn persistence across decades of growth has rendered that assumption (ii)_____, and recent scholarship instead regards informal work as a(n) (iii)_____ feature of these economies rather than a passing stage.
questions.explain: Clues: (i) is glossed by 'a transitional holdover destined to disappear': predict leftover. (ii): 'stubborn persistence' disproves that view: predict indefensible. (iii) is set against 'a passing stage' by 'rather than': predict lasting. Vestigial, untenable, entrenched. Trap: ephemeral in (iii) agrees perfectly with blank (i), the old view, but 'instead' and 'rather than a passing stage' say the new view is the opposite. Prescient and axiomatic would endorse the assumption the text says failed. Incidental does not oppose 'passing'. Definitions: vestigial = remaining as a trace of something disappearing; untenable = impossible to defend; axiomatic = self-evidently true; prescient = foreseeing; entrenched = firmly established; ephemeral = short-lived. Lesson: 'instead' means the later blank must reverse the earlier one, not echo it.

questions.stem: Few philosophers write with Hartley's (i)_____: her sentences are so compressed that a single paragraph can demand an hour of rereading. Yet this density is not mere (ii)_____; each qualification earns its place, and readers who persist discover that what first seemed (iii)_____ is in fact rigorously precise.
questions.explain: Clues: 'so compressed' defines (i): concision. 'Not mere ___' needs a negative explanation of difficulty that the writer rejects; 'each qualification earns its place' answers the charge of deliberate murk: obscurantism. (iii) is what the dense prose 'first seemed', contrasted with 'rigorously precise': impenetrable. Trap: prolixity sounds like a fault of hard prose, but prolixity means wordiness, which contradicts blank (i) and 'compressed'. Garrulity is the same opposite trap in (i). Transparent in (iii) reverses the 'first seemed' contrast. Definitions: concision = brevity of expression; garrulity = excessive talkativeness; levity = lightness, lack of seriousness; obscurantism = deliberately making things obscure; prolixity = tedious wordiness; exactitude = precision. Lesson: a fault the writer denies must still be the kind of fault the text's facts could suggest; compressed prose invites a charge of obscurity, not wordiness.

questions.stem: Critics who dismissed the painter's late canvases as the products of failing eyesight were (i)_____ the evidence: X-ray analysis shows that the apparently careless brushwork was laid over meticulous underdrawings, a sign that the painter's apparent (ii)_____ was deliberate. Far from a decline, then, the late style represents a(n) (iii)_____ choice.
questions.explain: Clues: the X-ray refutes the critics, so (i) is negative toward them: misreading. (ii) refers back to 'apparently careless brushwork': looseness. 'Far from a decline' plus 'deliberate' gives (iii): considered. Trap: precision in (ii) is right next to 'meticulous underdrawings', but the point is that the surface, which looks careless, was intended; 'apparent precision' would refer to nothing visible. Inadvertent in (iii) is the critics' view, contradicted by 'deliberate'. Corroborating would agree with critics the X-ray disproves. Definitions: corroborating = confirming; considered = carefully thought out; inadvertent = unintentional. Lesson: 'apparent' points to what the viewer sees on the surface; fill it with the surface quality, not the hidden one.

questions.stem: The court's opinion was notably (i)_____: rather than announcing a broad principle, the justices resolved the case on the narrowest available ground. Some commentators praised this (ii)_____ as appropriate judicial modesty; others complained that by declining to address the larger constitutional question, the court had merely (iii)_____ a reckoning that it would eventually have to face.
questions.explain: Clues: 'narrowest available ground' gives (i): limited, so circumscribed. 'Praised... as judicial modesty' gives (ii): restraint. (iii): 'merely ___ a reckoning that it would eventually have to face' means postponed: deferred. Trap: obviated sounds like a sophisticated word for 'avoided', but obviate means to make unnecessary, which contradicts 'would eventually have to face'. Precipitated (hastened) is the opposite. Sweeping contradicts 'narrowest'; activism contradicts 'modesty'; ambiguity is not what modesty praises. Definitions: circumscribed = restricted in scope; acrimonious = bitter; precipitated = brought on suddenly; obviated = made unnecessary, prevented. Lesson: check the end of the sentence; 'would eventually have to face' rules out any word meaning the problem is gone.

questions.stem: The early studies of the phenomenon were (i)_____ by small samples and lax controls, and when larger laboratories attempted to reproduce them, the effect (ii)_____. Proponents now concede that the original findings were, at best, (iii)_____, though they maintain that a subtler version of the effect may yet survive scrutiny.
questions.explain: Clues: small samples and lax controls weaken a study: (i) compromised. Replication by bigger labs of weak studies: the effect (ii) vanished: evaporated. 'Concede' plus 'at best' plus 'a subtler version may yet survive' means the findings were exaggerated but not worthless: (iii) overstated. Trap: fabricated is negative like the context, but 'at best fabricated' is incoherent, and proponents who still believe in a subtler effect would not concede fraud. Understated reverses direction: if the effect shrank on replication, it was exaggerated. Intensified and stabilized clash with the concession. Definitions: compromised = weakened, made unreliable; bolstered = supported. Lesson: 'at best' signals the mildest negative still compatible with the rest of the sentence; avoid the extreme option.

questions.stem: Historians once portrayed the Song dynasty as militarily (i)_____, a regime that bought peace with tribute because it could not win it on the battlefield. Yet this portrait (ii)_____ the dynasty's considerable innovations in naval warfare and gunpowder weaponry, and some scholars now argue that the payments reflected a(n) (iii)_____ calculation that tribute was cheaper than war, not mere weakness.
questions.explain: Clues: 'could not win it on the battlefield' gives (i): weak, feeble. 'Yet' introduces a correction: the portrait ignores the innovations: (ii) neglects. (iii) is glossed as 'tribute was cheaper than war, not mere weakness': a cool cost-benefit judgment, pragmatic. Trap: desperate in (iii) fits 'tribute' locally, but it restates the old view that 'not mere weakness' rejects. Exaggerates in (ii) is wrong because a portrait of weakness would not inflate military innovations; underscores would mean the portrait stresses them. Quixotic is the opposite of a calculation. Definitions: feeble = weak; quixotic = idealistic and impractical; pragmatic = practical, results-oriented. Lesson: when a sentence ends with 'not X', the blank must be the alternative to X, not a version of X.

questions.stem: The essayist makes no pretense of (i)_____; his chapters wander from botany to theology to his grandmother's kitchen without apology. What redeems the book is not its structure, which is (ii)_____, but its sentences, which are so (iii)_____ that the reader hardly minds where they lead.
questions.explain: Clues: 'wander... without apology' tells you what he does not pretend to: (i) order, system. 'Redeems... not its structure' says the structure is a weakness: (ii) haphazard. 'Redeems' and 'hardly minds where they lead' require (iii) to be strongly positive: beguiling. Trap: meandering fits 'wander' and 'where they lead' locally, but a meandering sentence would not redeem a meandering book; (iii) must be praise. Whimsy in (i) contradicts the wandering (he obviously has whimsy). Rigorous in (ii) contradicts (i). Definitions: haphazard = lacking order or plan; austere = severely plain; beguiling = charming, enchanting; meandering = winding, aimless; pedantic = overly concerned with minor detail and learning. Lesson: 'redeems' sets up a contrast; the redeeming blank must carry the opposite charge of the faults listed before it.

questions.stem: The central bank's new forecasting model is undeniably (i)_____ (it incorporates hundreds of variables and outperforms its predecessor on historical data), but its sophistication comes at a cost. Because few officials understand its inner workings, its projections are accepted with a (ii)_____ that would have been unthinkable for the simpler model, whose assumptions anyone could (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'hundreds of variables' and 'its sophistication' give (i): elaborate. The cost: no one understands it, so no one checks it; projections are accepted uncritically: (ii) credulity. The simpler model is the contrast: its assumptions anyone could (iii) question, interrogate. Trap: skepticism in (ii) seems natural ('few understand it, so they doubt it'), but then 'unthinkable for the simpler model whose assumptions anyone could interrogate' makes no sense; the simple model was the one that got scrutinized. Endorse in (iii) breaks the same contrast. Definitions: parsimonious = economical, using few elements (here, few variables); rudimentary = basic; credulity = readiness to believe without evidence; interrogate = question closely. Lesson: solve (ii) and (iii) as a pair; the old model's treatment must be the reverse of the new one's.

questions.stem: European artists who encountered Japanese woodblock prints in the 1860s were less faithful (i)_____ than opportunistic borrowers: they adopted flattened perspective and bold outlines while ignoring the prints' conventions of subject and format. This (ii)_____ reception tells us more about the Europeans' own preoccupations than about the Japanese tradition, which most of them understood only (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'less faithful ___ than opportunistic borrowers' contrasts complete copying with selective taking: (i) imitators. 'Adopted... while ignoring' makes the reception (ii) partial. 'Tells us more about the Europeans... than about the Japanese tradition' implies limited understanding: (iii) superficially. Trap: indiscriminate in (ii) sounds like a criticism and so fits the skeptical tone, but it means taking everything without selection, the opposite of 'adopted... while ignoring'. Profoundly contradicts the point that the borrowing reveals European, not Japanese, concerns. Detractors cannot be 'borrowers'. Definitions: partial = incomplete, selective (also biased); indiscriminate = unselective; grudgingly = reluctantly. Lesson: a word that matches the writer's tone can still contradict the writer's facts; test it against the description.

questions.stem: That the treatise was (i)_____ in its own century is no evidence of its insignificance; ideas that run too far ahead of their time are often ignored precisely because their contemporaries lack the concepts needed to (ii)_____ them. Only after later thinkers had independently arrived at similar conclusions was the work recognized as (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'no evidence of its insignificance' and 'often ignored' give (i): neglected. Ideas are ignored when people cannot understand them: (ii) comprehend. 'Ahead of their time' plus later thinkers 'arrived at similar conclusions' gives (iii): far-seeing, prescient. Trap: derivative in (iii) is tempting because the work resembles later conclusions, but it came first, so it is the later work that would be derivative. Refute in (ii) is locally sensible after 'lack the concepts', but inability to refute an idea leads to engagement, not neglect. Celebrated contradicts 'ignored'. Definitions: prescient = having foresight; derivative = imitative, unoriginal; obsolete = outdated. Lesson: track time order; an earlier work that matches later ideas anticipated them.

questions.stem: The documentary's portrait of the fishing village is (i)_____ to a fault: so determined is the filmmaker to avoid condescension that she never asks her subjects a difficult question. The result is a film whose warmth is genuine but whose insight is (ii)_____, an affectionate tribute that (iii)_____ rather than illuminates the community's troubles.
questions.explain: Clues: 'to a fault' plus 'never asks a difficult question' gives (i): excessively respectful, deferential. 'Warmth is genuine but insight is ___' requires a negative: (ii) meager. (iii) contrasts with 'illuminates': hides, glosses over. Trap: profound in (ii) is a natural partner for 'genuine', but 'but' demands a contrast and 'to a fault' frames the whole item as criticism. Lays bare is a synonym of 'illuminates', so 'lays bare rather than illuminates' is nonsense. Exacerbates is negative but a film cannot worsen the village's troubles. Intrusive and sardonic contradict avoiding condescension. Definitions: deferential = respectfully yielding; sardonic = mockingly scornful; meager = scant; acerbic = sharply bitter; gloss over = conceal by treating briefly; exacerbate = make worse. Lesson: '___ rather than Y' needs the opposite of Y, never a synonym.

questions.stem: Accounts of Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 dwell on his (i)_____, recounting how he distributed so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell for years. Such stories, however, have tended to (ii)_____ the administrative achievements of the empire he ruled, reducing a complex state to a single (iii)_____ image of a king scattering wealth.
questions.explain: Clues: 'distributed so much gold' defines (i): lavish generosity, munificence. 'However' plus 'reducing a complex state' gives (ii): overshadow, eclipse. (iii) describes a vivid but simplifying image: picturesque. Trap: piety in (i) is suggested by 'pilgrimage', but the clause after the comma explains what the accounts dwell on, and it is gold, not devotion. Parsimony is the opposite pair (stinginess). Prosaic in (iii) clashes with a king scattering gold; comprehensive contradicts 'reducing'. No outside knowledge needed; the text explains the gold. Definitions: munificence = great generosity; parsimony = extreme frugality; eclipse = overshadow; corroborate = confirm; picturesque = visually charming, colorful; prosaic = dull, ordinary. Lesson: the clause right after a blank usually defines it; do not answer from an association with the topic.

questions.stem: The jurist's argument is (i)_____ in the best sense: it builds from premises almost no one would dispute to a conclusion that almost everyone had, until now, rejected out of hand. This very strength, however, is also its weakness, since an argument that (ii)_____ every likely objection can seem to have been designed less to persuade than to (iii)_____ debate.
questions.explain: Clues: reaching a conclusion 'almost everyone had... rejected out of hand' from undisputed premises is bold: (i) audacious. 'This very strength' is the airtight construction: (ii) anticipates and blocks objections, forestalls. The weakness: it seems built to shut down discussion, (iii) foreclose. Trap: ignores in (ii) is a typical criticism, but the sentence calls it a strength first, and an argument that ignores objections is not strong. Foster in (iii) reverses the weakness; 'designed less to persuade than to foster debate' would be praise. Timid contradicts a conclusion everyone disputes. Definitions: audacious = boldly daring; forestall = prevent by acting in advance; foreclose = rule out, shut off. Lesson: 'this very strength is also its weakness' means one feature must fit both a positive and a negative blank; choose the word that can do both.

questions.stem: Because participants in the experiment knew they were being observed, their generosity may have been less (i)_____ than (ii)_____, a performance staged for the benefit of the researchers. To rule out this possibility, later investigators made their observations (iii)_____, and the generosity diminished markedly.
questions.explain: Clues: 'a performance staged for the researchers' defines (ii): theatrical. 'Less (i) than (ii)' needs the contrast: genuinely selfless, disinterested. To test whether being watched mattered, the observation must be hidden: (iii) covert; the drop in generosity confirms it. Trap: ostentatious in (i) fits 'performance' locally but puts the performance word on the rejected side of 'less... than'. Sincere in (ii) reverses the order. Conspicuous in (iii) would repeat the original flaw. Definitions: disinterested = unselfish, impartial (NOT uninterested); ostentatious = showy to impress; covert = hidden; sporadic = occasional. Lesson: in 'less X than Y', put the phrase the appositive defines in Y, and its opposite in X.

questions.stem: The biographer has unearthed a wealth of new documents, and her research is nothing if not (i)_____. Unfortunately, she seems unable to (ii)_____ any of it: every letter and receipt is reproduced at length, so that the subject's life disappears beneath a mass of (iii)_____ detail.
questions.explain: Clues: 'unearthed a wealth of new documents' gives (i): diligent, assiduous. 'Unfortunately' turns to a flaw: 'every letter and receipt is reproduced at length' means she does not select: (ii) winnow. A mass where nothing is sorted by importance: (iii) undifferentiated. Trap: authenticate in (ii) fits 'documents' locally, but the colon explains the flaw as over-inclusion, not doubtful sources. Telling in (iii) is praise and contradicts 'life disappears'. Fabricated contradicts genuine research. Slipshod reverses (i). Definitions: assiduous = diligent, persistent; slipshod = careless; tendentious = biased toward a cause; winnow = sift out the valuable from the worthless; undifferentiated = not sorted or distinguished; telling = revealing, significant. Lesson: the explanation after a colon names the exact flaw; pick the word for that flaw, not a generically plausible one.

questions.stem: Before the nineteenth century, Indian cotton textiles were so (i)_____ in European markets that English manufacturers lobbied for laws banning their import. The subsequent collapse of the Indian industry is thus difficult to attribute to any inherent (ii)_____ of its producers; more plausibly, it reflects (iii)_____ policies that favored British mills.
questions.explain: Clues: competitors lobbying for a ban implies the goods were in high demand: (i) coveted. 'Thus' links that success to (ii): if they were so competitive, the collapse is hard to blame on producer weakness: inefficiency. 'Policies that favored British mills' gives (iii): discriminatory. Trap: laissez-faire in (iii) sounds like a historical term for economic policy, but policies that 'favored' one side and an import ban are the opposite of free markets. Reviled and scarce do not explain a ban by rivals. Ingenuity in (ii) reverses the logic. Definitions: coveted = eagerly desired; reviled = hated; laissez-faire = noninterference by government in markets; benevolent = kindly. Lesson: 'thus' means the next blank follows from the first; if the industry was strong, the collapse cannot be blamed on weakness.

questions.stem: The sculptor's early work was criticized as (i)_____, a pastiche of styles borrowed from the masters she admired. In the retrospective, though, one sees that these borrowings were never (ii)_____; even in her student pieces, she bends each inherited idiom toward ends entirely her own, and the apparent eclecticism turns out to mask a(n) (iii)_____ sensibility.
questions.explain: Clues: 'a pastiche of styles borrowed' gives (i): derivative. 'Bends each inherited idiom toward ends entirely her own' shows the borrowings were never blind copies: (ii) slavish. 'Apparent eclecticism' masks a unified, original sensibility: (iii) singular. Trap: fragmented in (iii) matches 'eclecticism' locally, but 'apparent... turns out to mask' signals the reality is the reverse of the surface. Deliberate in (ii) contradicts 'bends... toward ends entirely her own', which is deliberate. Conventional contradicts 'entirely her own'. Iconoclastic reverses (i). Definitions: derivative = imitative; iconoclastic = attacking established beliefs; pastiche = work imitating others' styles; slavish = blindly imitative; eclecticism = drawing on varied sources; singular = unique, remarkable. Lesson: 'apparent X masks Y' requires Y to be the opposite of X.

questions.stem: The image of the Ottoman Empire in its final century as a (i)_____ power, the 'sick man of Europe', owes more to the hopes of its rivals than to sober assessment. The empire in fact undertook sweeping reforms of its army and bureaucracy, and its eventual collapse was hardly the (ii)_____ outcome that hindsight makes it seem; until the First World War, at least, its (iii)_____ was by no means assured.
questions.explain: Clues: 'sick man of Europe' glosses (i): dying, moribund. 'Hindsight makes it seem' a foregone conclusion: (ii) inevitable. The semicolon extends that point: the collapse was not certain, so its (iii) demise was not assured. Trap: survival in (iii) produces a sentence that sounds fine on its own ('survival was by no means assured'), but it would argue that the empire was in danger, which supports the 'sick man' view the author is rebutting. Improbable in (ii) reverses hindsight's effect. Resurgent contradicts 'sick'. Definitions: moribund = near death, in terminal decline; belligerent = warlike; demise = end, death. Lesson: a blank after a semicolon usually continues the author's claim; reject choices that quietly flip to the opposing view.

questions.stem: Critics of utilitarianism often charge that it is (i)_____ in theory but monstrous in practice, endorsing any act, however cruel, so long as it maximizes aggregate welfare. Defenders reply that this objection (ii)_____ the theory, which in its more sophisticated versions accounts for the (iii)_____ effects of cruelty on trust and social cohesion, effects that rarely appear in the philosopher's thought experiments.
questions.explain: Clues: 'in theory but monstrous in practice' requires (i) to be positive: elegant. Defenders reply that the objection misrepresents the theory by ignoring its refinements: (ii) caricatures. Cruelty's effect on trust is damaging: (iii) corrosive. Trap: ruthless in (i) agrees with 'monstrous' and the critics' hostility, but 'but' requires a contrast. Negligible in (iii) contradicts the defenders' point that sophisticated versions count those effects. Salutary reverses the effect. Vindicates would mean the objection proves the theory right. Definitions: caricature (verb) = represent in a distorted, exaggerated way; vindicate = justify, clear of blame; corrosive = gradually destructive; salutary = beneficial. Lesson: 'X in theory but Y in practice' always pairs opposites; check (i) against 'but' before matching its tone to the speaker.

questions.stem: The director has never been a (i)_____ storyteller; his plots stall and double back, and loose ends are left dangling. Nor does he care much for psychological (ii)_____: his characters remain ciphers whose motives we can only guess at. And yet few filmmakers have so (iii)_____ a command of image, and it is for the pictures, not the stories, that one returns.
questions.explain: Clues: 'plots stall and double back' says he is not (i) tightly controlled: disciplined. 'Nor' adds a second shortcoming: characters are 'ciphers', so he neglects (ii) depth. 'And yet... it is for the pictures that one returns' requires strong praise in (iii): assured. Trap: digressive in (i) describes his plots exactly, which is why it is wrong: 'never been a digressive storyteller' contradicts 'stall and double back'. Obscurity in (ii) likewise describes the characters and so cannot be what he does not care for. Tentative reverses the praise. Definitions: digressive = wandering from the main subject; prolific = producing much; cipher = a person of no individuality, or a puzzle; caprice = whim; assured = confident, sure. Lesson: after 'never' or 'nor', the blank is what he LACKS; a word that describes him is a trap.

questions.stem: Proponents of the minimum-wage increase predicted that its effects on employment would be (i)_____, and early data seemed to bear them out. Skeptics, however, warned that such effects are often (ii)_____, emerging only years later as firms gradually automate tasks rather than abruptly laying workers off; on this view, the early data, though accurate, were simply (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: proponents of a wage increase predict little job loss: (i) negligible. 'Emerging only years later' defines (ii): delayed. Accurate data that came too early to catch delayed effects: (iii) premature. Trap: transient in (ii) sounds like a time word, but it means short-lived, the reverse of effects that appear late. Definitive in (iii) is the proponents' view that skeptics dispute. Fraudulent contradicts 'though accurate'. Pronounced and catastrophic in (i) are what opponents, not proponents, would predict. Definitions: negligible = too small to matter; transient = lasting only briefly; premature = occurring too early. Lesson: time words are easy to confuse; 'emerging only years later' is about onset (delayed), not duration (transient).

questions.stem: A translator of classical Chinese poetry faces a(n) (i)_____: render the poems literally, and their compressed allusions become (ii)_____ to the modern reader; render them freely, and one risks substituting one's own voice for the poet's. The new translation steers between these hazards with rare tact, glossing allusions unobtrusively while preserving the originals' (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: two options, each with a cost, form a (i) dilemma ('these hazards' confirms). Literal rendering of compressed allusions leaves them (ii) unintelligible, which is why the translator must 'gloss' them. What should be preserved echoes 'compressed': (iii) terseness. Trap: verbosity is the opposite pair (like prolix vs taciturn) and contradicts 'compressed'. Ornamentation does not echo anything in the text. Transparent reverses the problem, and banal (commonplace) is not the risk of untranslated allusions; glossing fixes obscurity, not dullness. Definitions: sinecure = a job requiring little work; dilemma = choice between two undesirable options; banal = trite; terseness = brevity; verbosity = wordiness. Lesson: the solution described later (glossing) tells you the problem named earlier (unintelligibility).

questions.stem: Freud's theories are now widely regarded as (i)_____ by the standards of experimental science, resting on case studies that cannot be replicated. Yet to dismiss him entirely would be (ii)_____, for several of his central ideas, notably that much mental activity occurs outside awareness, have been (iii)_____ by research he could not have foreseen.
questions.explain: Clues: 'case studies that cannot be replicated' gives (i): unverifiable. 'Yet' and 'for' set up a defense: dismissing him would be (ii) hasty, rash, because his ideas were (iii) confirmed, vindicated. Trap: anticipated in (iii) sounds scholarly, but research he 'could not have foreseen' came after him; it confirmed his ideas rather than anticipating them. Discredited would support dismissal. Prudent in (ii) reverses the 'Yet'. Iconoclastic in (i) may be true of Freud, but it is not what non-replicable case studies imply about scientific standards. Definitions: iconoclastic = attacking cherished beliefs; rash = acting without careful thought; vindicated = proven right; discredited = shown to be false. Lesson: the reason clause after 'for' must support the judgment before it; test each pair together.

questions.stem: To viewers trained on Renaissance naturalism, Byzantine icons can look (i)_____: figures float against gold grounds, bodies are elongated, and perspective is often reversed. But these features were not failures of skill; they were (ii)_____ choices, intended to signal that the image depicted a realm beyond ordinary space and time. To judge them as (iii)_____ attempts at realism is thus to misunderstand their purpose.
questions.explain: Clues: to naturalism-trained eyes, floating, elongated figures look unnatural: (i) stilted. 'Not failures of skill' plus 'intended to signal' gives (ii) deliberate. The mistaken judgment is that they are failed realism: (iii) clumsy. Trap: arbitrary in (ii) seems to fit 'choices', but arbitrary means without reason, which contradicts 'intended to signal' a meaning. Opulent in (i) is suggested by 'gold grounds', but the list concerns distortion of form, and the viewer's complaint is unnaturalness, not richness. Successful in (iii) reverses the misjudgment. Definitions: stilted = stiff and unnatural; opulent = lavish, luxurious; inadvertent = unintentional; arbitrary = based on whim, not reason. Lesson: a single vivid detail (gold) can lure you; fill the blank with what the whole list has in common.

questions.stem: The statute's drafters intended its language to be (i)_____, so that judges would have little room to substitute their own preferences for the legislature's. In practice, however, the key term proved so (ii)_____ that courts in different jurisdictions reached flatly contradictory readings, and the law that was meant to (iii)_____ judicial discretion ended up expanding it.
questions.explain: Clues: 'little room' for judges means (i) clear: unambiguous. 'Contradictory readings' means the term was (ii) open to multiple meanings: equivocal. 'Meant to ___ discretion ended up expanding it' requires (iii) to oppose 'expanding': curtail. Trap: augment in (iii) is a synonym of 'expanding', so 'meant to augment... ended up expanding' loses the irony the 'however' sets up. Technical in (ii) is plausible for legal terms, but technical language does not explain contradictory readings. Elastic in (i) is what the term became, not what drafters intended. Definitions: equivocal = open to more than one interpretation; archaic = old-fashioned; curtail = reduce, restrict; augment = increase. Lesson: 'meant to X... ended up Y' is an irony structure; X and Y must be opposites.

questions.stem: The novelist's prose has been praised as (i)_____, and on the sentence level the praise is deserved: there is scarcely a wasted word. But economy at the level of the sentence is not the same as economy at the level of the book, and this one, at nearly seven hundred pages, is (ii)_____ in its plotting, pursuing subplots that (iii)_____ and then simply vanish.
questions.explain: Clues: 'scarcely a wasted word' gives (i): spare. 'But economy... is not the same' and 'seven hundred pages' make the plotting wasteful: (ii) profligate. Subplots that multiply 'and then simply vanish': (iii) proliferate. Trap: taut in (ii) carries over the praise of blank (i), but the 'But' sentence says the book lacks the sentences' economy. Perfunctory means done with minimal effort, which does not fit a sprawling seven-hundred-page plot. Converge and culminate imply resolution, contradicting 'simply vanish'. Florid contradicts 'no wasted word'. Definitions: spare = lean, economical; florid = overly ornate; mannered = artificial, affected; profligate = recklessly wasteful; perfunctory = done routinely, without care; proliferate = multiply rapidly. Lesson: when a reviewer splits praise and blame between levels (sentence vs book), keep each blank on its own side of the split.

questions.stem: Because the Inca had no system of writing in the conventional sense, early European observers assumed that their administration must have been (i)_____. The khipu, knotted cords used to record census and tribute data, reveal instead a bureaucracy of remarkable (ii)_____, one capable of tracking the obligations of millions of subjects with a precision that (iii)_____ that of many literate states of the period.
questions.explain: Clues: observers assumed no writing meant a primitive administration: (i) rudimentary. 'Instead' reverses that: (ii) sophistication, refinement. Precision 'that ___ that of many literate states' is a comparison: (iii) rivaled, equaled. Trap: byzantine in (i) means intricate, which is what the khipu actually reveal; putting it in (i) makes 'instead' meaningless. Despotic is unrelated to the absence of writing. Belied (contradicted) and emulated (imitated) do not express a comparison of quality; there is no claim the Inca copied anyone. Definitions: byzantine = excessively complicated; despotic = tyrannical; venality = corruptibility; belie = contradict, misrepresent; emulate = imitate in order to equal. Lesson: 'assumed... reveal instead' means blank (i) is the error and (ii) is the correction; never let the correction word leak into (i).

questions.stem: Popper's demand that scientific theories be falsifiable was meant to (i)_____ genuine science from pseudoscience. Critics have noted, though, that working scientists rarely abandon a theory at the first contrary observation; they more often (ii)_____ it with auxiliary hypotheses, a practice that Popper's criterion, applied strictly, would condemn as (iii)_____ but that has frequently proved fruitful.
questions.explain: Clues: 'from' and the purpose of a criterion give (i): separate, demarcate. Scientists 'rarely abandon' a theory; instead they (ii) support it with auxiliary hypotheses: shore up. A strict falsificationist would 'condemn' this as dodging refutation: (iii) evasive; 'but... fruitful' confirms (iii) is negative. Trap: jettison in (ii) is what Popper would want, but the sentence just said scientists rarely do it. Exemplary and innocuous cannot follow 'condemn as'. Conflate is the opposite of (i). Definitions: demarcate = set boundaries, distinguish; conflate = merge, confuse; shore up = prop up, support; jettison = discard; innocuous = harmless. Lesson: the verb governing a blank ('condemn as') fixes its charge before you read the choices.

questions.stem: Even the film's detractors concede that its battle sequences are (i)_____, staged with a scale and clarity few war films have matched. Their complaint is rather that this technical mastery serves a (ii)_____ vision of history, one in which the moral complexities of the conflict are (iii)_____ in favor of a tidy story of heroes and villains.
questions.explain: Clues: 'even the detractors concede' and 'few war films have matched' give (i) brilliant: bravura. 'A tidy story of heroes and villains' gives (ii) simplistic. Complexities dropped 'in favor of' a tidy story: (iii) omitted, elided. Trap: gratuitous in (i) is a common complaint about battle scenes and suits 'detractors', but 'concede' signals praise, and 'technical mastery' confirms it. Nuanced contradicts 'tidy'. Jaundiced (cynical) does not fit a heroes-and-villains story. Foregrounded and exaggerated contradict 'in favor of a tidy story'. Definitions: bravura = brilliantly skillful; pedestrian = dull; gratuitous = unnecessary, unjustified; jaundiced = bitter, cynical; elide = omit, pass over. Lesson: 'even critics concede' is a praise signal; do not let the speaker's identity pull the blank negative.

questions.stem: Classical economic models assume that consumers are (i)_____ calculators who weigh costs and benefits with perfect consistency. Behavioral economists have documented so many (ii)_____ from this ideal (people value a good more once they own it, for instance) that some argue the assumption should be abandoned; others reply that it remains a useful (iii)_____, valuable precisely because it is a simplification.
questions.explain: Clues: 'perfect consistency' gives (i): coolly rational, dispassionate. Documented exceptions 'from this ideal' are (ii) departures. 'Precisely because it is a simplification' defines (iii): approximation. Trap: fallacy in (iii) captures the critics' view that the assumption is false, but 'useful' and the defenders' framing make it incoherent. Certainty contradicts 'simplification' and the documented exceptions. Capricious and sentimental describe real people, not the model. Inferences and corollaries do not go with 'from this ideal' as evidence against it. Definitions: dispassionate = unemotional, impartial; capricious = unpredictable, whimsical; corollary = a proposition that follows from another; fallacy = a mistaken belief or invalid argument. Lesson: identify whose voice each blank belongs to; 'others reply' is the defenders, so (iii) must be favorable.

questions.stem: The author does not claim to be (i)_____: by his own admission he has consulted only English-language sources and has visited none of the archives in question. Within these limits, though, his synthesis is (ii)_____, drawing together scattered secondary literature into an argument of real force. Specialists will quarrel with details, but general readers could hardly ask for a more (iii)_____ introduction.
questions.explain: Clues: limited sources and no archives explain (i): he cannot claim to be the final word, authoritative. 'Within these limits, though' turns to praise: skillful, (ii) deft. 'Argument of real force' gives (iii) cogent. Trap: exhaustive in (ii) is positive, but it contradicts blank (i) and 'within these limits' (this is the classic comprehensive-vs-deft error). Definitive in (iii) does the same. Persuasive in (i) contradicts 'argument of real force'; readable contradicts 'general readers could hardly ask for more'. Definitions: deft = neatly skillful; exhaustive = complete, thorough; cogent = clear and convincing; tendentious = promoting a particular cause. Lesson: once the text admits a limit, every later praise word must stay inside that limit; reject praise for the very quality admitted missing.

questions.stem: Chinese literati painters of the Yuan period deliberately cultivated a(n) (i)_____ manner, eschewing the polished brushwork of court artists in favor of dry, seemingly careless strokes. To them, technical (ii)_____ smacked of the professional craftsman who painted for money, whereas a certain studied awkwardness signaled the (iii)_____ of a scholar who painted only for himself and his friends.
questions.explain: Clues: 'eschewing the polished brushwork' gives (i): unpolished. What the court professional had was (ii) technical brilliance: virtuosity. The scholar who paints 'only for himself' shows freedom from commercial motive: (iii) detachment. Trap: incompetence in (iii) echoes 'awkwardness', but 'studied' awkwardness is deliberate and signals status, not lack of skill. Clumsiness in (ii) reverses the contrast; it belongs to the literati, not to the craftsman. Avarice belongs to the professional 'who painted for money'. Definitions: eschew = deliberately avoid; ornate = elaborately decorated; virtuosity = great technical skill; austerity = severe plainness; avarice = greed; detachment = aloofness from worldly concerns. Lesson: in 'whereas' sentences, assign each blank to the correct side of the contrast before choosing.

questions.stem: Eyewitnesses are often most (i)_____ precisely when they are least accurate: confidence, research shows, is a poor guide to the reliability of a memory. This finding is (ii)_____ to jurors, who tend to regard a witness's certainty as strong evidence, and it has led some courts to (iii)_____ juries about the fallibility of recollection.
questions.explain: Clues: the colon says confidence is a poor guide, so (i) is a word for confident: adamant. Jurors trust certainty, so the finding goes against their expectation: (ii) counterintuitive. Courts respond by warning juries: (iii) caution. Trap: diffident is the opposite pair (shy, unsure); 'most diffident when least accurate' would make confidence a good guide, contradicting the colon. Self-evident in (ii) contradicts jurors' belief. Reassure in (iii) reverses the courts' purpose. Equivocal (noncommittal) also contradicts 'certainty'. Definitions: adamant = unshakably insistent; diffident = lacking self-confidence; equivocal = ambiguous; counterintuitive = contrary to common-sense expectation; fallibility = liability to err. Lesson: when a paradox ('most X when least accurate') is explained after a colon, fill X with the quality the colon names.

questions.stem: The Meiji reformers' embrace of Western institutions is sometimes described as wholesale imitation, but this account is (i)_____. The reformers borrowed (ii)_____, adopting a German-style constitution, a French legal code, and a British-model navy, each chosen for its fit with Japanese aims. Their approach, in short, was less (iii)_____ than eclectic.
questions.explain: Clues: 'but' rejects 'wholesale imitation': (i) misleading. 'Each chosen for its fit' gives (ii) with careful selection: discriminatingly. 'Less ___ than eclectic' needs the rejected label, wholesale imitation: (iii) slavish. Trap: indiscriminately in (ii) looks similar to the answer but means without selection, which is the account the passage rejects. Selective and pragmatic in (iii) are true descriptions of the reformers, so they cannot sit on the rejected side of 'less... than'. Compelling contradicts 'but'. Definitions: discriminatingly = with careful judgment; indiscriminately = without distinction; slavish = copying without originality; eclectic = drawing from diverse sources. Lesson: 'less X than Y' needs X to be the view the passage rejects; a true description in X is a trap.

questions.stem: The philosopher's new book on moral luck is admirably (i)_____, never claiming more for its arguments than they can bear; where earlier writers on the topic issued grand pronouncements, she offers careful, (ii)_____ conclusions. If the book has a fault, it is that this caution sometimes shades into (iii)_____, so that the reader finishes uncertain what, if anything, she actually believes.
questions.explain: Clues: 'never claiming more... than they can bear' gives (i) cautious: circumspect. Opposed to 'grand pronouncements' and paired with 'careful': (ii) qualified, hedged. 'This caution... shades into' a fault that leaves us unsure what she believes: (iii) evasiveness. Trap: dogmatism and bombast in (iii) are standard faults of philosophy books, but a fault that grows out of caution and leaves the reader uncertain must be noncommittal, not overconfident. Sweeping in (ii) is the earlier writers' vice. Grandiose and dogmatic contradict 'admirably' and 'never claiming more'. Definitions: circumspect = wary, prudent; hedged = qualified, limited; incendiary = inflammatory; bombast = pompous, inflated language. Lesson: in mixed reviews the fault is usually the virtue taken too far; extend the praised quality, do not reverse it.

questions.stem: Defenders of the tariff argued that protection would (i)_____ the nation's infant industries until they could compete on their own. Critics did not dispute the logic so much as its (ii)_____: protected industries, they observed, rarely seemed to grow up, and the temporary shelter tended to become (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'until they could compete on their own' gives (i): nurture. 'Did not dispute the logic so much as its ___' needs something other than the logic itself: how it worked out in practice, application. The observation that industries 'rarely grow up' and the contrast with 'temporary' give (iii) permanent. Trap: premise and validity in (ii) are parts of the logic, which the critics explicitly did not dispute. Obsolete in (iii) sounds like a negative outcome but contradicts 'industries rarely grow up'; the shelter never stopped being needed. Precarious means unstable, also not opposed to 'temporary'. Definitions: nurture = care for and foster growth; stifle = suppress; premise = a proposition an argument rests on. Lesson: 'not X so much as Y' requires Y to be outside X; reject choices that are parts of X.

questions.stem: Her early poems were (i)_____ to the point of opacity, crowded with private allusions that even sympathetic readers struggled to decode. The new collection is far more (ii)_____, yet it has lost none of the earlier work's intensity; the plainness, it turns out, was not a (iii)_____ but a distillation.
questions.explain: Clues: 'private allusions' and 'opacity' give (i): sealed, hermetic. 'Far more' signals change and 'the plainness' names it: (ii) accessible. 'Lost none of the intensity' means the plainness did not weaken her work; 'not a ___ but a distillation' needs the opposite of distillation: dilution. Trap: refinement in (iii) is nearly a synonym of distillation, so 'not a refinement but a distillation' says nothing. Recondite in (ii) describes the early poems, not the new ones. Limpid is the opposite pair in (i). Definitions: hermetic = obscure, closed to outsiders; limpid = clear; recondite = obscure, little known; dilution = weakening; distillation = extraction of the essential. Lesson: 'not A but B' requires A and B to be opposites; a near-synonym of B is always wrong.

questions.stem: Laws against vagrancy were ostensibly (i)_____, prohibiting a condition rather than any particular act, and thus applying in principle to anyone. In practice, their very vagueness made them instruments of (ii)_____ enforcement, wielded against whichever groups the authorities found inconvenient. It was this gap between their (iii)_____ language and their selective application that finally led courts to strike them down.
questions.explain: Clues: 'ostensibly' plus 'applying in principle to anyone' gives (i): neutral. 'In practice' turns it: used against whatever groups were inconvenient means (ii) arbitrary enforcement. 'The gap between their ___ language and their selective application' needs (iii) to restate (i): impartial. Trap: uniform in (ii) restates the 'in principle' side and kills the 'in practice' contrast. Inflammatory and archaic in (iii) are negative or merely descriptive, but the 'gap' needs the language to be the fair-sounding side. Punitive is true of laws generally but not what 'applying to anyone' explains. Definitions: ostensibly = apparently, as claimed; punitive = intended as punishment; arbitrary = based on whim, not rule; lenient = mild; impartial = treating all equally. Lesson: 'gap between X and Y' means X and Y are opposites; (iii) should echo blank (i), not blank (ii).

questions.stem: The architect's museum is (i)_____ from the street, a blank stone wall offering passersby no hint of what lies within. Inside, however, the building opens into a sequence of luminous galleries whose generosity is all the more striking for the (ii)_____ of the facade. Some visitors find the contrast exhilarating; others find the exterior merely (iii)_____, a snub to the city rather than a prelude to the art.
questions.explain: Clues: 'a blank stone wall offering no hint' gives (i): forbidding. 'All the more striking for' a contrast with luminous generosity gives (ii) plainness, austerity. 'A snub to the city' gives (iii): aloof. Trap: transparency in (ii) is a word associated with 'luminous galleries', but the facade is a blank wall. Exuberance reverses the contrast. Welcoming in (iii) contradicts 'snub'. Gaudy (flashy) contradicts 'blank stone wall', and ornate in (i) does the same. Definitions: forbidding = unfriendly, threatening; austerity = severe simplicity; exuberance = lively abundance; aloof = distant, cold; gaudy = tastelessly showy. Lesson: 'all the more striking for' signals that the blank is the opposite of the quality being praised.

questions.stem: Historians once treated medieval Islamic astronomers as mere (i)_____ of Greek learning, preserving Ptolemy's work until Europe was ready to receive it. This view has proved (ii)_____: astronomers at Maragha and elsewhere developed mathematical models that corrected Ptolemy's flaws, and some of their techniques (iii)_____ devices later used by Copernicus.
questions.explain: Clues: 'mere' plus 'preserving' gives (i): keepers, custodians. The colon offers evidence against the view: corrections and new models show it is too simple, (ii) reductive. Techniques that came before similar ones 'later used' by Copernicus: (iii) prefigured. Trap: innovators in (i) is what the passage argues they were, so it cannot be the old view that 'mere' introduces. Supplanted in (iii) sounds strong but gets time backward; an earlier technique cannot replace a later device. Prescient and uncontroversial would endorse the old view. No knowledge of Maragha is needed. Definitions: custodian = guardian, keeper; reductive = oversimplifying; prefigure = anticipate, foreshadow; supplant = replace. Lesson: 'mere' marks the dismissive old view; the old view's blank must be the modest word.

questions.stem: The psychologist's account of willpower is engaging and often (i)_____, full of observations that make familiar behavior suddenly strange. But its central claim rests on experiments that others have failed to replicate, and the author's (ii)_____ about their findings now looks (iii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'engaging' plus 'make familiar behavior suddenly strange' gives (i) illuminating. 'But' turns to criticism: the book's central claim rests on the experiments, so the author trusted them, (ii) confidence; failed replications make that trust look (iii) premature. Trap: skepticism plus warranted (or prescient) forms a smooth pair on its own, but an author whose central claim rests on those experiments was not skeptical of them, and the 'But' requires a criticism of the author. Ambivalence is unsupported. Tedious contradicts 'engaging'. Definitions: illuminating = clarifying, revealing; dubious = doubtful; ambivalence = mixed feelings; premature = too early, hasty; warranted = justified; prescient = foreseeing. Lesson: two blanks can agree with each other and still break the passage; check the pair against the signal word ('But') and the facts.

questions.stem: Microfinance was hailed in the 1990s as a(n) (i)_____ for global poverty, a way to lift millions into self-sufficiency through small loans. Rigorous evaluations have since tempered that enthusiasm: the loans appear to help some borrowers smooth their consumption, but their effect on long-term income is (ii)_____. The lesson is not that microfinance is (iii)_____ but that it is a modest tool, not a transformative one.
questions.explain: Clues: 'hailed' and 'lift millions' give (i): cure-all, panacea. 'Tempered that enthusiasm' plus 'but' after a modest benefit gives (ii) small: marginal. 'Not that it is ___ but that it is a modest tool' needs the extreme on the other side from transformative: worthless. Trap: palliative in (i) accurately describes the evaluations' finding (relief without cure), so it cannot be what the 1990s enthusiasts 'hailed'. Transformative in (iii) is already rejected at the end of the sentence, making it redundant. Indispensable is praise. Dramatic contradicts 'tempered'. Definitions: panacea = remedy for all ills; palliative = something that relieves symptoms without curing; scourge = cause of great suffering; marginal = minor. Lesson: when a sentence corrects two extremes, each blank takes one extreme; do not put the middle view in either.

questions.stem: The adaptation is scrupulously (i)_____ to its source, reproducing whole passages of the novel's dialogue verbatim. Yet fidelity of this kind can be a form of (ii)_____: what reads as wit on the page sounds stagy when spoken aloud, and the filmmakers' reluctance to alter a word leaves the actors (iii)_____ by lines never meant to be heard.
questions.explain: Clues: 'reproducing... verbatim' gives (i) faithful, confirmed by 'fidelity'. 'Yet... can be a form of' sets up a paradox: fidelity that harms the work is (ii) betrayal. Actors stuck with lines meant for reading are (iii) hampered: hamstrung. Trap: homage in (ii) is the natural partner of 'fidelity', but 'Yet' and the colon's list of harms require the paradoxical negative. Liberated and enraptured contradict 'stagy' and 'reluctance to alter a word'. Irreverent and indifferent contradict 'scrupulously' and 'verbatim'. Definitions: scrupulously = with great care; verbatim = word for word; irreverent = disrespectful; homage = public respect; hamstrung = severely restricted. Lesson: 'X can be a form of ___' after 'Yet' almost always wants the paradoxical opposite of X.

questions.stem: Akbar's religious tolerance is often presented as a(n) (i)_____ commitment, rooted in personal conviction. Some historians, however, see in it a more (ii)_____ motive: ruling a predominantly Hindu population as a Muslim emperor, he had every reason to (iii)_____ the loyalty of his non-Muslim subjects.
questions.explain: Clues: 'rooted in personal conviction' glosses (i): principled. 'However' and the political reasoning after the colon make (ii) self-interested, a means to an end: instrumental. A minority ruler had reason to (iii) win and keep loyalty: secure. Trap: tactical in (i) is the revisionist reading, the very view introduced by 'however', so it cannot describe the conventional account. Spiritual and altruistic in (ii) restate the conviction view. Jeopardize and disregard in (iii) contradict 'every reason to'. The answer comes from the colon's reasoning, not from knowledge of Mughal history. Definitions: tepid = lukewarm, half-hearted; instrumental = serving as a means to an end; altruistic = unselfish. Lesson: when two views are contrasted, label each blank by whose view it belongs to before matching words.
