questions.stem: The critic's essays are neither (i)_____ nor systematic; she proceeds by hunches, and her conclusions are often more suggestive than demonstrable. But it would be a mistake to call her (ii)_____, for her hunches are disciplined by an extraordinarily wide reading, and her apparent (iii)_____ conceals a deep familiarity with the texts she discusses.
questions.explain: Clues: (i) pairs with 'systematic' and contrasts with 'hunches' and 'more suggestive than demonstrable': rigorous. 'It would be a mistake to call her ___, for... extraordinarily wide reading' needs a charge of shallowness: (ii) dilettantish. 'Apparent ___ conceals a deep familiarity' needs a surface look of offhandedness: (iii) casualness. Trap: intuitive in (i) describes her exactly ('proceeds by hunches'), so 'neither intuitive' contradicts the text. Erudite in (ii) is true of her, so calling her erudite would not be a mistake. Pedantry and severity are the opposite of a hunch-driven manner. Definitions: dilettantish = superficially dabbling; erudite = learned; pedantry = excessive display of learning. Lesson: 'it would be a mistake to call her X, for [evidence]' means X is refuted by the evidence; never choose the word the evidence supports.

questions.stem: The Great Depression was long blamed on the stock market crash of 1929, but most economists now regard the crash as more (i)_____ than cause. In their view, what turned an ordinary downturn into a catastrophe was the central bank's (ii)_____: rather than expanding the money supply as banks failed, it allowed that supply to (iii)_____ by nearly a third.
questions.explain: Clues: 'more ___ than cause' needs a non-cause: symptom. 'Rather than expanding... it allowed' describes failure to act: (ii) passivity. 'Rather than expanding' requires the opposite in (iii): contract ('by nearly a third' confirms a change). Trap: catalyst in (i) sounds sophisticated, but a catalyst is a kind of cause, so 'more catalyst than cause' undercuts the contrast. Profligacy (wasteful spending) contradicts 'rather than expanding'. Balloon contradicts the same phrase; stabilize contradicts 'by nearly a third'. Remedy contradicts 'catastrophe'. Definitions: catalyst = something that triggers change; profligacy = reckless extravagance; contract = shrink. Lesson: 'rather than X, it allowed Y' makes Y the opposite of X; read the 'rather than' clause first and the blank becomes easy.

questions.stem: Early photographers anxious to have their medium accepted as art often (i)_____ painting, smearing their lenses and retouching negatives to achieve soft, brushlike effects. Later critics would judge these efforts (ii)_____, arguing that photography came into its own only when it stopped apologizing for its (iii)_____ and embraced the sharp, mechanical detail that no painter could match.
questions.explain: Clues: smearing lenses for 'brushlike effects' to be 'accepted as art' gives (i): imitated, emulated. 'Came into its own only when it stopped' doing this makes (ii) negative: misguided. What photography was 'apologizing for' is what it later 'embraced': sharp detail, (iii) precision. Trap: vagueness in (iii) refers to the smeared effects, but those were the apology, not the thing apologized for; the text says it later embraced sharpness. Visionary and audacious in (ii) contradict 'only when it stopped'. Disparaged contradicts the imitation; supplanted overstates. Definitions: emulate = imitate in order to match; disparage = belittle; supplant = replace. Lesson: 'stopped apologizing for X and embraced X' means X is the same quality both times; check that (iii) matches what follows 'embraced'.

questions.stem: In his study of boredom, the author resists the temptation to treat his subject as either a(n) (i)_____ complaint, beneath serious notice, or a profound existential condition. Instead he charts a middle course, showing how ordinary tedium can be (ii)_____ yet revealing. The approach is sensible, but the book itself occasionally (iii)_____ the very state it describes.
questions.explain: Clues: 'beneath serious notice' defines (i): trivial; it is the opposite pole from 'profound existential condition'. The 'middle course' joins both poles: (ii) everyday, mundane, 'yet revealing'. 'Sensible, but' sets up a reservation, and 'the very state it describes' (boredom) points to an ironic fault: the book (iii) induces boredom. Trap: dispels in (iii) is positive, which the 'but' rules out. Disdains is negative but makes no sense for a book that studies boredom seriously. Grave in (i) contradicts 'beneath serious notice'. Exalted and tragic in (ii) belong to the 'profound' pole, not the middle course. Definitions: mundane = ordinary, everyday; exalted = elevated; disdain = scorn; induce = bring about. Lesson: 'the very X it describes' signals irony; the blank usually makes the work do the thing it studies.

questions.stem: The demands of _____ notwithstanding, the reviewers argued that a fuller account of the sampling method, even at the cost of several additional pages, would have spared readers considerable confusion.
questions.explain: Clue: "notwithstanding" means the blank names a demand that pulls AGAINST the reviewers' wish for "a fuller account... several additional pages." Predict: shortness. Economy (in its secondary sense, economy of words) and concision both mean saying things briefly. Trap: thoroughness and exhaustiveness are a real synonym pair, but they point the wrong way; thoroughness would support a fuller account, not oppose it. Space fits the sentence on its own ("the demands of space") but has no partner. Lucidity is the clarity trap: clarity is not the same as brevity, and a fuller account would serve clarity. Definitions: economy = efficient use, here of words; concision = brevity; exhaustiveness = completeness; lucidity = clearness. Lesson: in SE, find the pair that means the SAME thing; a word that merely fits the topic (clarity, space) is not enough.

questions.stem: Far from endorsing the theory wholesale, the reviewer chose to _____ her praise, conceding its elegance while noting that its predictions had been tested only on a handful of laboratory populations.
questions.explain: Clue: "far from endorsing... wholesale" plus "conceding... while noting" shows praise given but limited. Predict: limit or moderate. Qualify (secondary sense: to limit or restrict a statement) and temper (to moderate) both mean she gave praise with reservations. Trap: amplify and magnify are a synonym pair in the opposite direction; they contradict "far from endorsing wholesale." Reserve sounds right but means withhold for later, yet she did concede elegance, so some praise was given; no partner anyway. Retract means take back praise already given, which the sentence never says. Definitions: qualify = limit, add reservations to; temper = moderate, soften; amplify = enlarge. Lesson: ETS loves the secondary meaning of qualify: limit, not certify.

questions.stem: The new drug does not so much reverse the degeneration of retinal cells as _____ it: patients rarely regain lost vision, but those treated early seldom lose more.
questions.explain: Signal: "not so much X as Y" says Y replaces X. The colon explains: no vision regained (not reversal), but "seldom lose more" (the decline stops). Predict: halt. Arrest (secondary sense: stop a process) and stem (stop the flow of) both mean halt. Trap: accelerate and hasten are synonyms but say the drug speeds the damage, the opposite of "seldom lose more." Mitigate fits loosely (lessen severity) but lessening is not stopping, and it has no partner. Diagnose is unrelated to treatment outcomes. Definitions: arrest = halt; stem = stop, check; mitigate = make less severe; hasten = speed up. Lesson: arrest and stem are classic secondary meanings; read the colon for the exact degree (stop, not slow).

questions.stem: Although the memoir has been praised for its vivid portraits of the author's contemporaries, readers seeking any sustained reflection on her own motives will find it sadly _____.
questions.explain: Signal: "Although... praised" sets up a shortcoming; "sadly" confirms something is missing, namely reflection on her motives. Predict: lacking. Wanting (secondary sense: lacking, inadequate) and deficient both mean the book falls short in this respect. Trap: replete and abundant are a synonym pair meaning full, the opposite direction. Evasive fits the sentence on its own (she may dodge her motives) but describes intent, not absence, and has no partner. Prolix (wordy) does not address the missing reflection. Definitions: wanting = lacking; deficient = insufficient; replete = filled; evasive = avoiding directness; prolix = tediously wordy. Lesson: "wanting" on the GRE almost always means lacking, not desiring.

questions.stem: Critics who dismiss the composer as a mere imitator of his teachers overlook the _____ quality of his late quartets, whose harmonic language has no real precedent in the music of his era.
questions.explain: Clue: "has no real precedent" and the contrast with "mere imitator." Predict: unique, remarkable. Singular (secondary sense: exceptional, unlike others) and unparalleled both say nothing else compares. Trap: derivative and imitative are synonyms, but they repeat the critics' view the sentence rejects. Mature fits grammatically (late quartets) but does not answer "no precedent" and has no partner. Solitary is the sounds-related trap: singular does not mean alone here. Definitions: singular = remarkable, unique; unparalleled = without equal; derivative = copied from others. Lesson: singular on the GRE usually means extraordinary, not merely one.

questions.stem: Far from the frugal steward his admirers describe, the duke was _____ with the estate's revenues, financing three palaces and a private opera company within a decade.
questions.explain: Signal: "Far from the frugal steward" means the truth is the opposite of frugal, and the evidence is lavish spending on palaces and an opera company. Predict: wasteful. Prodigal and profligate both mean recklessly extravagant. Trap: parsimonious and miserly are a synonym pair, but they restate "frugal," the view the sentence rejects. Generous fits on its own but implies giving to others, not waste, and has no partner. Scrupulous (careful, honest) contradicts the point. Definitions: prodigal = wastefully extravagant; profligate = recklessly wasteful; parsimonious = stingy; scrupulous = careful about correctness. Lesson: "far from X" means the answer is the opposite of X; the trap pair is usually a synonym of X.

questions.stem: Although the council had never formally _____ the practice, it had for years treated it as settled policy, so residents were startled to learn that the practice had no legal standing at all.
questions.explain: Signal: "Although" sets the blank against "treated it as settled policy," and the result clause, "no legal standing," tells you what was missing: formal approval. Predict: approved. Sanctioned (here: officially approved) and authorized match. Trap: proscribed and interdicted are a synonym pair meaning forbade; "never forbade it" would not explain why the practice lacks legal standing. Documented fits loosely but has no partner; investigated likewise. Definitions: sanction = approve (it can also mean penalize); proscribe = forbid; interdict = prohibit. Lesson: sanction has two opposite meanings; let the result clause choose which one.

questions.stem: The trade body's _____ against members who falsified emissions data were so mild that several firms reportedly treated the fines as an ordinary cost of doing business.
questions.explain: Clue: "against members who falsified data" and "the fines" show punishments. Predict: penalties. Sanctions (here: penalties for breaking rules) and penalties match. Trap: endorsements and approvals are synonyms and match the OTHER meaning of sanction (approve), which a learner who knows only one sense may reach for; they cannot be "against" wrongdoers and are not fines. Warnings fits the sentence on its own but is not a fine and has no partner. Inquiries are investigations, not punishments. Definitions: sanction = penalty (or approval, depending on context); endorsement = public support. Lesson: "sanctions against" means penalties; "sanctioned by" usually means approved.

questions.stem: Her reputation as a _____ collector rests less on the size of her holdings than on her uncanny ability to distinguish a minor master's genuine work from the competent forgeries that flooded the market.
questions.explain: Signal: "less on X than on Y": the reputation rests on Y, her ability to "distinguish" real from fake. Predict: perceptive, good at judging. Discriminating (secondary sense: showing fine judgment) and discerning both fit. Trap: voracious and insatiable are synonyms, but they describe appetite for quantity, which the sentence explicitly downplays ("less on the size of her holdings"). Wealthy fits as a description of a collector but has no partner and misses the clue. Biased is the sounds-related trap, the negative sense of discriminate. Definitions: discriminating = discerning, selective; voracious = greedy for more. Lesson: discriminating on the GRE is usually a compliment: able to tell fine differences.

questions.stem: The economist's enthusiasm for the reform was _____ by her recognition that its benefits, though real, would accrue chiefly to households already well above the median income.
questions.explain: Clue: "though real" shows she still values the reform, but the benefits going to the well-off is a drawback. Enthusiasm is therefore reduced, not destroyed. Predict: softened. Tempered and moderated both mean lessened in intensity. Trap: intensified and heightened are a synonym pair in the wrong direction; a drawback does not increase enthusiasm. Complicated fits on its own but has no partner. Hardened is the sounds-related trap: to temper steel is to harden it, but tempering enthusiasm means softening it. Definitions: temper = moderate; accrue = accumulate. Lesson: when a concession ("though real") is present, choose a word of partial reduction, not reversal.

questions.stem: In the framers' design, each branch of government was meant to _____ the ambitions of the others, so that no single faction could accumulate power unopposed.
questions.explain: Clue: "so that no single faction could accumulate power unopposed" shows the purpose is restraint. Predict: restrain. Check (secondary sense: to hold back) and curb both mean restrain. Trap: abet and foster are synonyms meaning encourage, which would help factions accumulate power. Monitor fits loosely (watching) but watching does not oppose, and it has no partner. Verify is the sounds-related trap for check (as in "check a fact"). Definitions: check = restrain; curb = limit, restrain; abet = encourage, assist (often in wrongdoing); foster = promote. Lesson: check in academic prose often means restrain, as in "checks and balances."

questions.stem: The placid surface of the novel's prose _____ the violence of the events it recounts, a dissonance some readers find unsettling and others merely evasive.
questions.explain: Clue: "dissonance" signals a mismatch between placid prose and violent events. Predict: hides or contradicts. Belies (gives a false impression of) and disguises both say the calm style conceals the violence; "evasive" supports concealment. Trap: reflects and mirrors are a synonym pair, but calm prose cannot mirror violence; that removes the dissonance. Heightens fits on its own (understatement can intensify), but it has no partner, and "evasive" points to hiding. Corroborates (confirms) is wrong. Definitions: belie = misrepresent, contradict; corroborate = confirm. Lesson: belie means to give a false picture of; it is a concealment word, not a revealing one.

questions.stem: The historian's revision is not so much a refutation of the earlier account as a _____ of it: she accepts its central chronology but adds the economic context its author ignored.
questions.explain: Signal: "not so much a refutation as a Y" plus the colon: she "accepts" the chronology and "adds" context. Predict: an addition. Supplement and augmentation both mean something added to complete or enlarge. Trap: repudiation and rejection are synonyms, but they restate "refutation," the option the sentence sets aside. Critique fits on its own (she notes what was ignored), but the colon stresses adding, and critique has no partner. Paraphrase means restating, not adding. Definitions: augmentation = enlargement; repudiation = rejection, disowning. Lesson: in "not so much X as Y," the trap pair is usually a synonym of X.

questions.stem: The committee's report did little to allay public anxiety about the reactor; if anything, its studiously vague language _____ suspicions that serious faults were being concealed.
questions.explain: Signal: "did little to allay; if anything" means the effect went the other way: suspicion increased. Predict: increased. Fueled and stoked both mean fed, intensified. Trap: allayed and assuaged are synonyms meaning calmed, the very effect the sentence says did NOT occur. Confirmed fits the sentence on its own, but vague language cannot really confirm anything, and confirmed has no partner. Documented is unrelated. Definitions: allay = calm, relieve; assuage = soothe; stoke = feed a fire, intensify. Lesson: "if anything" pushes the meaning beyond the negation into the opposite direction.

questions.stem: Unlike most specialists of his generation, who confined themselves to a single period, the critic was strikingly _____ in his tastes, writing with equal enthusiasm about medieval chant and postwar jazz.
questions.explain: Clue: "Unlike... confined themselves to a single period" and "equal enthusiasm about medieval chant and postwar jazz." Predict: wide-ranging. Catholic (lowercase, secondary sense: universal, broad) and eclectic both mean drawing from many sources. Trap: parochial and provincial are synonyms meaning narrow, the specialists' habit he is contrasted with. Fervent fits ("equal enthusiasm") but misses breadth and has no partner. Orthodox is the sounds-related trap from Catholic as a religion. Definitions: catholic = broad in scope; eclectic = varied; parochial = narrow-minded. Lesson: lowercase catholic means universal; it has nothing to do with religion on the GRE.

questions.stem: Though the translation is scrupulously accurate, its prose is so _____ that readers unfamiliar with the original would never guess why the poem has been revered for centuries.
questions.explain: Signal: "Though... accurate" sets up a fault; readers "would never guess why the poem has been revered," so the prose is dull. Predict: dull, uninspired. Pedestrian (secondary sense: ordinary, lacking imagination) and prosaic match. Trap: lyrical and mellifluous are synonyms in the opposite direction; beautiful prose would reveal the poem's greatness. Literal fits on its own (an accurate translation is often literal) but means word-for-word, not dull, and has no partner. Ambulatory is the sounds-related trap (walking). Definitions: pedestrian = dull; prosaic = commonplace; mellifluous = sweetly flowing. Lesson: pedestrian is an ETS favorite for uninspired.

questions.stem: Having seen two earlier compounds fail in late-stage trials, the firm's investors were understandably _____ of committing further capital to a drug whose mechanism remained poorly understood.
questions.explain: Clue: two earlier failures and a "poorly understood" mechanism make caution "understandable." Predict: cautious. Chary and wary both mean cautious, reluctant. Trap: eager and avid are synonyms but contradict "understandably"; past failures do not justify enthusiasm. Weary of fits idiomatically but means tired of, a different meaning, and is the sounds-related trap for wary; no partner. Ignorant contradicts the sentence (they know the history). Definitions: chary = cautiously reluctant; wary = on guard; avid = keen. Lesson: when a sounds-alike word (weary/wary) fits, test whether it keeps the same meaning as the others.

questions.stem: The infection proved _____ to every antibiotic the clinicians tried, forcing them to fall back on an experimental phage therapy.
questions.explain: Clue: "forcing them to fall back on an experimental" therapy means the antibiotics failed. Predict: resistant. Refractory (resistant to treatment) and impervious (not affected by) both fit. Trap: susceptible and vulnerable are a synonym pair, but if the infection responded, no fallback would be needed. Inimical fits grammatically ("inimical to") but means harmful or hostile to, so it says the infection damages antibiotics, not that it resists them; no partner. Subsequent makes no sense. Definitions: refractory = stubbornly resistant; impervious = unaffected; inimical = harmful, hostile. Lesson: a consequence clause ("forcing them to...") tells you the direction of the blank.

questions.stem: So thoroughly documented is the decline of the region's pollinator populations that even the industry's own scientists no longer attempt to _____ it, preferring instead to dispute its causes.
questions.explain: Clue: "so thoroughly documented" that they "no longer attempt to" do X, and instead "dispute its causes." X is disputing the decline itself. Predict: deny. Gainsay and controvert both mean deny or contradict. Trap: corroborate and substantiate are synonyms meaning confirm; heavy documentation would not stop anyone from confirming. Measure fits grammatically but has no partner and misses the contrast. Explain is tempting, but explaining a decline means discussing its causes, which they still do. Definitions: gainsay = deny; controvert = argue against; corroborate = confirm. Lesson: "no longer X, preferring instead Y" means X and Y are parallel actions; here both are forms of disputing.

questions.stem: The manifesto is less a coherent program than a(n) _____ collection of grievances, its authors agreeing on what they oppose but not on what they would build in its place.
questions.explain: Signal: "less a coherent program than" means the blank is the opposite of coherent; the explanation follows: no agreement on what to build. Predict: unformed, shapeless. Inchoate (not fully formed) and amorphous (shapeless) match. Trap: systematic and methodical are synonyms that restate "coherent," the quality denied. Incendiary fits on its own (grievances can be inflammatory) but has no partner and ignores the coherence contrast. Eloquent is unrelated to structure. Definitions: inchoate = just begun, undeveloped; amorphous = without definite form; incendiary = inflammatory. Lesson: "less X than Y" means Y is chosen over X; the trap pair repeats X.

questions.stem: Volcanologists caution that a mountain which has been _____ for centuries is not necessarily extinct; the magma chamber beneath it may simply be recharging.
questions.explain: Clue: "not necessarily extinct" implies it only looks dead; "simply recharging" shows it is inactive for now. Predict: inactive, at rest. Quiescent and dormant both mean temporarily inactive. Trap: active and eruptive are synonyms but make the caution pointless; no one would think an erupting mountain extinct. Stable fits loosely but has no partner and does not mean inactive. Inaccessible is unrelated. Definitions: quiescent = at rest, inactive; dormant = sleeping, temporarily inactive. Lesson: the caution "X is not necessarily Y" requires X to resemble Y on the surface.

questions.stem: Readers who expect a philosopher of such reputation to write in a dense, allusive style are often surprised by the _____ prose of her essays, which a bright undergraduate can follow without difficulty.
questions.explain: Clue: "surprised" contrasts with "dense, allusive," and "a bright undergraduate can follow" it. Predict: clear. Pellucid and limpid both mean transparently clear in style. Trap: abstruse and recondite are synonyms meaning hard to understand, the expectation that was overturned. Elegant fits on its own but describes grace, not clarity, and has no partner. Terse (brief) is not the same as clear. Definitions: pellucid = translucently clear; limpid = clear, easily understood; abstruse = obscure; recondite = little known, profound. Lesson: "surprised" signals a reversal of the expectation just stated.

questions.stem: The discovery of the compound's antifungal properties was entirely _____: a technician investigating an unrelated reaction noticed that contaminated plates near the sample stayed clean.
questions.explain: Clue: the colon explains the blank: the technician was "investigating an unrelated reaction" and happened to notice. Predict: by chance. Fortuitous (happening by chance) and accidental match. Trap: deliberate and premeditated are synonyms meaning planned, the opposite. Fortunate fits on its own and is the sounds-related trap: it means lucky, which describes the value of the discovery, not its chance origin; no partner. Contested is unsupported. Definitions: fortuitous = by chance (not necessarily lucky); premeditated = planned in advance. Lesson: fortuitous means accidental; do not confuse it with fortunate.

questions.stem: The reformers did not claim that the city's inspectors were incompetent; their charge was rather that the inspectors were _____, routinely overlooking violations in exchange for cash or favors.
questions.explain: Clue: "in exchange for cash or favors" defines the blank. Signal: "not... incompetent; rather" shifts from skill to honesty. Predict: bribable. Venal and corruptible both mean open to bribery. Trap: incorruptible and upright are synonyms in the opposite direction. Negligent fits "overlooking violations" but ignores the payment and has no partner; it is also close to "incompetent," which the sentence rejects. Venial is the sounds-related trap: it means pardonable. Definitions: venal = willing to be bribed; venial = minor, forgivable; upright = honest. Lesson: venal (for sale) vs venial (forgivable) is a classic GRE pair.

questions.stem: Despite the board's insistence that the audit had been rigorous, its two-page summary suggested a _____ review, one that had sampled few transactions and questioned none.
questions.explain: Signal: "Despite... rigorous" means the truth is the opposite; "sampled few transactions and questioned none" confirms. Predict: superficial. Perfunctory and cursory both mean hasty and superficial. Trap: meticulous and painstaking are synonyms that restate "rigorous," the board's claim the sentence rejects. Partisan fits as a criticism of an audit but has no partner and is not supported by the details. Clandestine (secret) is unsupported. Definitions: perfunctory = done as a routine duty, with little care; cursory = hasty, not thorough. Lesson: "despite the claim X" means the blank contradicts X.

questions.stem: Because the trial's results were _____, the regulators declined either to approve the vaccine or to halt its development, requesting instead a larger study.
questions.explain: Clue: neither approval nor halt, and "a larger study" requested: the results settled nothing. Predict: unclear. Equivocal (open to more than one interpretation) and inconclusive match. Trap: decisive and definitive are synonyms; clear results would lead to approval or halt. Disappointing fits on its own but would push toward a halt, and has no partner. Falsified results would end the study, not extend it. Definitions: equivocal = ambiguous; definitive = final, conclusive. Lesson: when the consequence is "neither A nor B," look for a word meaning undecided.

questions.stem: Those who knew the general only from his _____ dispatches, rarely more than a line or two, were astonished by the expansive, almost garrulous memoir he published in retirement.
questions.explain: Clue: "rarely more than a line or two" and the contrast with "expansive, almost garrulous." Predict: brief. Laconic and succinct both mean using few words. Trap: verbose and prolix are synonyms meaning wordy, which describe the memoir, not the dispatches; no astonishment would follow. Infrequent fits on its own but describes how often, not how long, and has no partner. Candid is unrelated. Definitions: laconic = terse; succinct = briefly expressed; prolix = tediously long; garrulous = excessively talkative. Lesson: a contrast word ("astonished") means the blank is the opposite of what follows.

questions.stem: Negotiators had expected the union to yield on at least the pension question, but its leaders proved _____, rejecting every compromise the mediators put forward.
questions.explain: Signal: "expected... to yield, but" and "rejecting every compromise." Predict: unyielding. Intransigent and obdurate both mean stubbornly refusing to change. Trap: tractable and pliant are synonyms meaning easily managed, which is the expectation the "but" overturns. Militant fits on its own (aggressive) but has no partner and does not mean refusing compromise. Vocal is unrelated. Definitions: intransigent = refusing to compromise; obdurate = stubbornly persistent; tractable = easily controlled; pliant = flexible. Lesson: "expected X, but" usually points to the opposite of X.

questions.stem: Given the steady erosion of the coastline over the past decade, the engineers' _____ forecast that the seawall would protect the town for another century struck many residents as naive.
questions.explain: Clue: "naive" and "protect the town for another century" despite "steady erosion." Predict: overly hopeful. Sanguine and optimistic match. Trap: dire and grim are synonyms meaning gloomy, which cannot be naive given the erosion and do not fit "protect... another century." Precise fits grammatically but has no partner and does not explain "naive." Sanguinary is the sounds-related trap: it means bloody. Definitions: sanguine = cheerfully optimistic; sanguinary = bloodthirsty; dire = dreadful. Lesson: sanguine (hopeful) and sanguinary (bloody) look alike but mean very different things.

questions.stem: The negotiations, which had proceeded in a _____ fashion for months, with delegates meeting irregularly and often leaving early, acquired sudden urgency after the border incident.
questions.explain: Clue: "meeting irregularly and often leaving early" and the contrast with "sudden urgency." Predict: aimless, lacking enthusiasm. Desultory (lacking plan or enthusiasm) and halfhearted match. Trap: vigorous and energetic are synonyms, but they clash with leaving early and with "sudden urgency" coming later. Secretive fits the topic of negotiations but has no partner and ignores the clues. Cordial (friendly) is unsupported. Definitions: desultory = unfocused, without enthusiasm; halfhearted = lacking commitment. Lesson: an appositive phrase ("with delegates meeting irregularly") is a built-in definition of the blank.

questions.stem: Nineteenth-century physicians routinely sent consumptive patients to mountain towns whose thin, dry air was thought to be _____, though there was little evidence that it improved survival.
questions.explain: Clue: physicians "sent" patients there, and "though... little evidence that it improved survival" means the air was believed to help health. Predict: health-giving. Salubrious and healthful match. Trap: noxious and deleterious are synonyms meaning harmful; doctors would not send patients to harmful air. Bracing fits on its own (refreshing) but does not mean health-improving, and has no partner. Salutatory is the sounds-related trap: it means expressing a greeting. Definitions: salubrious = promoting health; deleterious = harmful; bracing = invigorating. Lesson: "though there was little evidence" concedes that a belief was positive.

questions.stem: The pamphlet presents itself as an impartial survey of the evidence, but its selective citations and loaded vocabulary reveal it to be thoroughly _____.
questions.explain: Signal: "presents itself as impartial... but" and the clues "selective citations" and "loaded vocabulary." Predict: biased. Tendentious (promoting a particular point of view) and partisan match. Trap: evenhanded and dispassionate are synonyms that restate "impartial," the pose the sentence exposes. Superficial fits selective citation loosely but has no partner and ignores "loaded vocabulary." Tedious is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: tendentious = biased toward a cause; dispassionate = free of emotion or bias. Lesson: "presents itself as X, but" means the answer is the opposite of X.

questions.stem: Although the treatise addresses questions that might seem _____ to most readers, its author's gift for illustration makes even its discussion of medieval tax law surprisingly absorbing.
questions.explain: Signal: "Although" and "surprisingly absorbing" mean the questions would seem unappealing; "medieval tax law" suggests obscure. Predict: obscure. Recondite and arcane both mean known only to a few. Trap: riveting and engrossing are synonyms meaning absorbing, which kills the "although... surprisingly" contrast. Tedious fits the sentence well on its own (tax law is dull) but has no partner among the choices; arcane means obscure, not boring. Venerable (respected for age) does not set up a contrast. Definitions: recondite = little known, abstruse; arcane = mysterious, specialized. Lesson: if one word fits perfectly but has no synonym, it is not the answer.

questions.stem: The courtier's _____ manner, so pleasing to the aging king, earned him the contempt of the other ministers, who saw in his constant flattery a calculated bid for advancement.
questions.explain: Clue: "constant flattery" and "pleasing to the aging king." Predict: fawning. Obsequious and sycophantic both mean excessively eager to please. Trap: imperious and haughty are synonyms meaning arrogant; arrogance would not please the king or be described as flattery. Charming fits the sentence on its own but is neutral or positive and has no partner; the contempt points to servility. Reticent (reserved) contradicts "constant flattery." Definitions: obsequious = servile, fawning; sycophantic = flattering for advantage; imperious = domineering. Lesson: a defining phrase later in the sentence ("constant flattery") outweighs a vague positive word ("pleasing").

questions.stem: Much of the period's most popular verse proved _____, admired by one generation and unread by the next, whereas the poems its contemporaries dismissed have since entered the canon.
questions.explain: Clue: "admired by one generation and unread by the next" and the contrast with poems that "entered the canon." Predict: short-lived. Ephemeral and evanescent both mean quickly fading. Trap: enduring and perennial are synonyms describing the canonical poems, the other side of "whereas." Derivative fits as a criticism of popular verse but has no partner and does not mean short-lived. Ethereal is the sounds-related trap: it means delicate or heavenly. Definitions: ephemeral = lasting a short time; evanescent = vanishing; perennial = lasting. Lesson: "whereas" pairs two opposites; do not take the word describing the other half.

questions.stem: To her critics, the scientist's decades-long search for a single unifying principle behind all animal behavior seemed _____, a noble but impractical quest unlikely ever to succeed.
questions.explain: Clue: the appositive defines the blank: "a noble but impractical quest unlikely ever to succeed." Predict: idealistic and unrealistic. Quixotic and utopian both mean idealistic to the point of impracticality. Trap: pragmatic and hardheaded are synonyms meaning practical, the opposite of "impractical." Obsessive fits "decades-long" but misses "noble" and has no partner. Fraudulent contradicts "noble." Definitions: quixotic = romantically unrealistic (from Don Quixote); utopian = idealistic, impossibly perfect; hardheaded = practical, realistic. Lesson: an appositive after a comma often restates the blank; use all of its parts ("noble" and "impractical").

questions.stem: Far from fostering innovation, the patent regime's endless litigation proved _____ to it, diverting to legal fees the capital that small firms might otherwise have spent on research.
questions.explain: Signal: "Far from fostering" means the opposite of fostering; "diverting... capital" from research shows harm. Predict: harmful. Inimical and detrimental both mean harmful to. Trap: conducive and propitious are synonyms meaning favorable, which restate "fostering." Irrelevant fits grammatically and avoids fostering, but the diversion of capital shows actual harm, not neutrality; no partner. Inured (accustomed to hardship) does not fit. Definitions: inimical = hostile, harmful; conducive = helpful to; propitious = favorable. Lesson: "far from X" usually wants the opposite of X, not merely the absence of X.

questions.stem: Though her scholarship was formidable, the young professor was so _____ in seminars that students often mistook her reluctance to assert her views for a lack of them.
questions.explain: Clue: "reluctance to assert her views" and "Though her scholarship was formidable." Predict: shy, unassertive. Diffident (lacking self-confidence, modest) and self-effacing (keeping oneself in the background) match. Trap: brash and brazen are synonyms meaning boldly forward, the opposite; this is the diffident vs gregarious mix-up. Aloof fits on its own (distant), but aloofness is coldness, not reluctance to assert, and it has no partner. Pedantic (showing off learning) contradicts the clue. Definitions: diffident = timid, modest; brash = rudely bold; brazen = shameless. Lesson: diffident means shy; the clue "reluctance to assert" decides it.

questions.stem: The second edition improves on the first chiefly by excision: the author has pruned the _____ digressions that once buried his argument, and the book is now half its former length.
questions.explain: Clue: "excision," "pruned," "buried his argument," and "half its former length." Predict: long-winded. Prolix and verbose both mean using too many words. Trap: pithy and concise are synonyms in the opposite direction; you would not need to prune concise passages. Erudite (learned) fits the sentence on its own, since learned digressions can still be cut, but has no partner. Polemical (argumentative) is unsupported. Definitions: prolix = tediously lengthy; verbose = wordy; pithy = brief and meaningful; excision = cutting out. Lesson: this is the prolix vs taciturn family; check whether the text wants more words or fewer.

questions.stem: The argument's _____ appeal lies in its use of genuine statistics; only on close inspection does one notice that the figures compare populations that differ in nearly every relevant respect.
questions.explain: Clue: the appeal exists, but "only on close inspection" is the flaw revealed. Predict: attractive on the surface but false. Specious (plausible but wrong) and meretricious (superficially attractive but without real value) match. Trap: veracious and truthful are synonyms meaning honest, the opposite; this is the specious vs veracious mix-up. Immediate fits on its own (the appeal is immediate, the flaw comes later) but has no partner and does not convey falseness. Spacious is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: specious = seemingly sound but false; meretricious = showily attractive but hollow; veracious = truthful. Lesson: specious is negative: it looks right but is not.

questions.stem: Although the poet drew her imagery from the most _____ sources, such as grocery lists, bus schedules, and the instructions on medicine bottles, her poems achieve a strangeness that few more ornate writers can match.
questions.explain: Clue: the examples (grocery lists, bus schedules) are ordinary, and "Although" contrasts them with the poems' strangeness. Predict: everyday. Prosaic (commonplace) and quotidian (daily, ordinary) match. Trap: esoteric and abstruse are synonyms meaning obscure, the opposite; this is the esoteric vs prosaic mix-up. Unlikely fits the sentence well on its own (these are unlikely sources for poetry) but has no partner. Ornamental contradicts the examples and the contrast with "ornate writers." Definitions: prosaic = dull, ordinary; quotidian = everyday; esoteric = understood by few. Lesson: examples given in the sentence are the strongest clue; match the word to them.

questions.stem: The empire reached its _____ under the third emperor, whose campaigns doubled its territory; within a century of his death, much of that territory had been lost.
questions.explain: Clue: "doubled its territory" and the later loss show a high point followed by decline. Predict: peak. Apogee and zenith both mean highest point. Trap: nadir and perigee are both lowest or nearest points, the opposite; this is the apogee vs perigee mix-up. Maturity fits on its own but does not imply the high point before decline, and it has no partner. Terminus means end point, which does not match doubled territory. Definitions: apogee = highest point (originally of an orbit); zenith = peak; nadir = lowest point; perigee = nearest point of an orbit to Earth. Lesson: apo- = away, far (high); peri- = near (low).

questions.stem: The biographer is careful not to excuse her subject's financial dealings, yet she insists that they reflect carelessness rather than _____, noting that he lost far more through them than he ever gained.
questions.explain: Signal: "carelessness rather than X": X is a moral fault worse than carelessness, which she denies. Predict: wickedness. Turpitude and depravity both mean moral corruption. Trap: probity and rectitude are synonyms meaning integrity; "carelessness rather than integrity" would be an accusation, not a defense; this is the turpitude vs propriety mix-up. Greed fits on its own (he lost more than he gained) but has no partner. Ineptitude is nearly the same as carelessness, so it cannot be its contrast. Definitions: turpitude = depravity, baseness; probity = honesty; rectitude = moral correctness. Lesson: "X rather than Y" means Y is the alternative being rejected; it must differ from X.

questions.stem: Contrary to the legend of the dissolute artist, the painter's letters reveal a man of _____ habits, who rose at dawn, drank little, and rarely left his studio before nightfall.
questions.explain: Signal: "Contrary to the legend of the dissolute artist" and the clue "drank little." Predict: restrained, moderate. Abstemious (sparing in food and drink) and temperate match. Trap: intemperate and debauched are synonyms that restate "dissolute," the legend the letters refute. Industrious fits the sentence (rarely left his studio) but has no partner and does not address "drank little." Eccentric is unsupported. Definitions: abstemious = moderate in eating and drinking; temperate = self-restrained; dissolute = indulgent in vice; debauched = morally corrupt. Lesson: when a detail like "drank little" appears, pick the word that captures it, not one that captures a side detail.

questions.stem: Though the scientist was _____ in the popular press as a lone genius, her own papers credit a large team of technicians whose contributions she considered indispensable.
questions.explain: Clue: "as a lone genius" is praise; "Though" contrasts the press's flattering picture with her own crediting of others. Predict: praised. Lionized and celebrated match. Trap: vilified and maligned are synonyms meaning attacked; being called a genius is not an attack. Portrayed fits the sentence perfectly on its own but is neutral and has no partner among the choices; lionized and celebrated alone produce the same meaning. Plagiarized makes no sense. Definitions: lionize = treat as a celebrity; vilify = speak ill of; malign = slander. Lesson: a neutral word that fits is still wrong without a synonym; SE rewards the pair.

questions.stem: Regulators faulted the firm less for the leak itself than for its _____ response, which consisted of a brief statement minimizing the danger and no attempt to notify nearby residents.
questions.explain: Clue: "minimizing the danger and no attempt to notify" shows a careless, dismissive attitude. Predict: dismissive. Cavalier (showing arrogant lack of concern) and offhand (casual, careless) match. Trap: conscientious and scrupulous are synonyms meaning careful, the opposite. Belated fits on its own (a slow response is common criticism) but nothing says it was late, and it has no partner. Chivalrous is the sounds-related trap: a cavalier was a knight, but cavalier the adjective is negative. Definitions: cavalier = dismissive; offhand = casual; scrupulous = careful. Lesson: the description after "which" is your definition.

questions.stem: The newly discovered letters do not _____ the minister entirely, but they show that he objected to the policy in private long before he was forced to defend it in public.
questions.explain: Clue: private objection to the policy is evidence in his favor; "not entirely... but" means partly clearing him. Predict: clear of blame. Exculpate and exonerate both mean free from blame. Trap: incriminate and inculpate are synonyms meaning implicate, the opposite; the letters help him. Rehabilitate fits on its own (restore reputation), but it is about reputation rather than blame and has no partner. Expatriate is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: exculpate = clear of guilt; exonerate = absolve; inculpate = accuse, blame; expatriate = exile. Lesson: ex-culpa = out of blame; in-culpa = into blame.

questions.stem: The reviewer's praise was so _____ that it embarrassed even the author, who confessed that she could not recognize her modest first novel in his effusions.
questions.explain: Clue: praise that "embarrassed" the author and the word "effusions"; she could not recognize her "modest" novel. Predict: excessive. Fulsome (secondary sense: excessive, overdone) and extravagant match. Trap: grudging and tepid are synonyms meaning half-hearted, which would not embarrass by excess. Sincere fits on its own but does not explain the embarrassment and has no partner. Fulfilling is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: fulsome = excessively flattering; extravagant = beyond reasonable limits; tepid = lukewarm; effusion = gushing expression. Lesson: fulsome praise is too much praise, not generous praise.

questions.stem: Knowing the siege might last through the winter, the garrison's commander resolved to _____ the remaining grain, issuing half rations even to his officers.
questions.explain: Clue: a long siege and "half rations" show careful saving. Predict: save. Husband (secondary sense: use sparingly) and conserve match. Trap: squander and dissipate are synonyms meaning waste, the opposite. Distribute fits on its own (he does hand out rations) but misses the point of saving, and it has no partner. Requisition (demand for official use) fits loosely but has no partner and does not mean ration. Definitions: husband (verb) = manage economically; dissipate = waste, scatter; requisition = officially demand supplies. Lesson: husband as a verb means to economize; ETS uses it for resources.

questions.stem: Admirers of the architect's early, ornate villas were dismayed by the _____ style of her later work, in which unadorned concrete walls met at sharp right angles.
questions.explain: Clue: "unadorned concrete walls" and the contrast with "early, ornate villas." Predict: plain. Spare (secondary sense: lean, unadorned) and austere match. Trap: florid and baroque are synonyms meaning elaborate, the style of the early villas. Monumental fits on its own (concrete buildings) but has no partner and does not mean plain. Surplus is the sounds-related trap: spare can mean extra, but not here. Definitions: spare = simple, lean; austere = severely plain; florid = elaborately decorated; baroque = highly ornate. Lesson: spare describing style means minimal, not extra.

questions.stem: The influence of the school _____ steadily through the 1950s, reaching its height just as its founders began to question the principles that had made it popular.
questions.explain: Clue: "steadily... reaching its height" means rising. Predict: grew. Waxed (secondary sense: increased, as the moon waxes) and swelled match. Trap: waned and ebbed are synonyms meaning declined, the opposite; something declining does not reach its height. Shifted fits grammatically but has no partner and does not mean grew. Polished is the sounds-related trap from waxing a floor. Definitions: wax = grow; wane = decline; ebb = recede. Lesson: wax and wane are opposites; "reaching its height" decides the direction.

questions.stem: Although trained as an engineer, he had always had a philosophical _____, and his late essays on the ethics of automation are read more widely than any of his technical papers.
questions.explain: Clue: "Although trained as an engineer" contrasts training with natural tendency; his philosophical essays succeeded. Predict: tendency. Bent (secondary sense: natural inclination) and inclination match. Trap: aversion and antipathy are synonyms meaning dislike; someone with an aversion to philosophy would not write widely read philosophical essays. Mentor fits on its own grammatically but has no partner. Warp is the sounds-related trap for bent as "crooked." Definitions: bent = natural talent or inclination; aversion = strong dislike; antipathy = hostility. Lesson: "a bent for" means a tendency; it is not about shape.

questions.stem: By the fourth hour of the debate, even the most energetic delegates had begun to _____, and the chair adjourned the session before the final resolution could be read.
questions.explain: Clue: "fourth hour," "even the most energetic," and the adjournment imply exhaustion. Predict: weaken. Flag (secondary sense: lose energy) and tire match. Trap: rally and revive are synonyms meaning regain energy, which gives no reason to adjourn. Dissent fits on its own (delegates disagreeing) but has no partner and ignores "even the most energetic." Signal is the sounds-related trap for flag as a banner or signal. Definitions: flag = decline in vigor; rally = recover strength. Lesson: "even the most X" points to the loss of X.

questions.stem: The occupying army _____ heavy tribute from the conquered provinces, and the resentment this produced outlasted the occupation itself by several generations.
questions.explain: Clue: "heavy tribute from the conquered" and lasting "resentment." Predict: demanded and took. Exacted (secondary sense: demanded and obtained by force) and extracted match. Trap: forgave and waived are synonyms meaning cancelled; cancelled tribute would not cause resentment, and "from" does not fit. Recorded fits grammatically but has no partner and explains nothing. Calibrated is the sounds-related trap for exact as "precise." Definitions: exact (verb) = demand and enforce payment; waive = give up a claim. Lesson: exact as a verb means to demand; it is not about precision.

questions.stem: Rather than inventing a new visual vocabulary, the movement's painters _____ the imagery of advertising, stripping slogans and logos from their commercial context and placing them in galleries.
questions.explain: Signal: "Rather than inventing" and the clue "stripping... and placing them in galleries." Predict: took over for their own use. Appropriated (secondary sense: took for one's own use) and co-opted match. Trap: shunned and eschewed are synonyms meaning avoided, which contradicts placing the images in galleries. Parodied fits on its own (pop art often mocks) but nothing says mockery, and it has no partner. Apportioned is the sounds-related trap: it means divided up. Definitions: appropriate (verb) = take; co-opt = adopt for one's own purpose; eschew = avoid. Lesson: appropriate as a verb means seize, not suitable.

questions.stem: Whatever its other merits, the proposal violates the _____ rule of field archaeology: that no site should be excavated faster than its findings can be recorded.
questions.explain: Clue: "Whatever its other merits" implies this violation is serious; the rule stated is basic to the discipline. Predict: chief. Cardinal (secondary sense: of greatest importance) and fundamental match. Trap: peripheral and incidental are synonyms meaning minor, which would undercut "whatever its other merits." Unwritten fits on its own but has no partner and says nothing about importance. Crimson is the sounds-related trap for cardinal as a color or a bird. Definitions: cardinal = primary, chief; peripheral = marginal; incidental = minor. Lesson: cardinal before rule, sin, or virtue means most important.

questions.stem: Whether the treaty was ever legally binding remains a _____ point among historians, since the only surviving copy lacks the seals that would settle the matter.
questions.explain: Clue: "remains... since... lacks the seals that would settle the matter" means the question is unsettled. Predict: open to argument. Moot (secondary sense: open to debate) and debatable match. Trap: indisputable and incontrovertible are synonyms meaning beyond dispute, the opposite of unsettled. Sensitive fits on its own but has no partner and does not follow from missing seals. Mute is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: moot = debatable (in American usage it can also mean irrelevant, which the "since" clause rules out); incontrovertible = undeniable. Lesson: a "since" clause gives the reason; pick the word the reason actually supports.

questions.stem: The diarist's _____ account of court intrigue, which takes every courtier's protestations at face value, is valuable precisely because its author lacked the cunning to edit what she saw.
questions.explain: Clue: "takes every courtier's protestations at face value" and "lacked the cunning." Predict: naive, innocent. Ingenuous and artless both mean innocent and unsophisticated. Trap: calculating and crafty are synonyms for cunning, which she lacked. Detailed fits on its own but has no partner and ignores the clues. Ingenious is the sounds-related trap: it means clever, nearly the opposite of ingenuous. Definitions: ingenuous = innocent, naive; artless = without guile; ingenious = inventive. Lesson: ingenuous (naive) vs ingenious (clever) is a top GRE confusion; check the clue.

questions.stem: Observers expecting the defendant to break down under cross-examination were struck by his _____ demeanor; he answered each accusation in the same flat, unhurried voice.
questions.explain: Clue: "expecting... to break down" contrasts with "the same flat, unhurried voice." Predict: unemotional. Stolid and impassive both mean showing no emotion. Trap: agitated and overwrought are synonyms meaning upset, which is what observers expected but did not see. Defiant fits the sentence on its own but implies resistance or anger, not flatness, and has no partner. Solid is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: stolid = calm, unemotional; impassive = expressionless; overwrought = extremely agitated. Lesson: the semicolon explains the blank; match its details (flat, unhurried).

questions.stem: For a nation so dependent on foreign trade, its intellectual life was curiously _____, its universities rarely inviting foreign scholars and its presses seldom translating foreign books.
questions.explain: Clue: "curiously" signals a surprise given dependence on trade, and the examples show a closed attitude to foreign ideas. Predict: inward-looking. Insular and parochial both mean narrow, uninterested in outside ideas. Trap: cosmopolitan and worldly are synonyms describing what one would expect of a trading nation, not what was found. Stagnant fits on its own but has no partner and is not about openness to foreign ideas. Peninsular is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: insular = narrow-minded, isolated; parochial = provincial; cosmopolitan = worldly, international. Lesson: "curiously" signals the opposite of what context would predict.

questions.stem: The commission's purpose was not to punish those responsible for the expropriations but to _____ the injustice done to the families who had lost their land.
questions.explain: Signal: "not to punish... but to" means a remedy focused on the victims. Predict: correct, remedy. Redress and rectify both mean set right. Trap: compound (secondary sense: make worse) and exacerbate are synonyms meaning worsen, which no commission would aim at. Document fits on its own (commissions record injustices) but has no partner. Dress is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: redress = remedy a wrong; rectify = correct; compound = intensify, make worse; exacerbate = aggravate; expropriation = seizure of property. Lesson: compound on the GRE often means worsen, not combine.

questions.stem: The historian does not _____ her predecessors' integrity; she argues only that their access to the archives was too limited for their conclusions to be trusted.
questions.explain: Signal: "does not X... she argues only that" means she makes a narrower criticism than X. X must be a harsher attack on integrity. Predict: attack. Impugn and assail both mean attack or challenge. Trap: vindicate and uphold are synonyms meaning defend; "she does not defend their integrity, only says their access was limited" makes "only" illogical. Discuss fits grammatically but has no partner. Impute is the sounds-related trap: it means attribute. Definitions: impugn = call into question; assail = attack; vindicate = clear, justify. Lesson: "not X; only Y" means X is a stronger version of Y.

questions.stem: Having spent his youth as a fervent advocate of central planning, the economist _____ those views in middle age, and his later work defends markets with a convert's zeal.
questions.explain: Clue: "with a convert's zeal" defending markets means a complete reversal. Predict: rejected. Abjured and renounced both mean formally gave up. Trap: espoused and embraced are synonyms meaning adopted, which describes his youth, not middle age. Qualified (secondary sense: limited) is tempting, but a convert does not merely limit his old views; no partner either. Adjured is the sounds-related trap: it means urged solemnly. Definitions: abjure = renounce; espouse = adopt, support; adjure = command solemnly. Lesson: the degree word ("convert's zeal") separates total reversal from mere qualification.

questions.stem: The restaurant critic found the much-praised dish _____, its delicate seasoning so restrained that the flavors of its individual ingredients could scarcely be detected.
questions.explain: Clue: "so restrained that the flavors... could scarcely be detected." Predict: tasteless. Insipid and bland both mean lacking flavor. Trap: piquant and pungent are synonyms meaning sharply flavored, the opposite. Subtle fits on its own (delicate seasoning) but is a compliment and has no partner; "scarcely detected" is a criticism. Overrated fits "much-praised" but has no partner and does not describe the flavor. Definitions: insipid = flavorless, dull; piquant = pleasantly sharp; pungent = strong-smelling or tasting. Lesson: when two loners both fit, the answer is still the pair that means the same thing.

questions.stem: The conductor's notoriously _____ temperament, cordial at one rehearsal and savage at the next, made the orchestra's players reluctant to raise even minor concerns with him.
questions.explain: Clue: "cordial at one rehearsal and savage at the next" shows unpredictability. Predict: changeable. Mercurial and volatile both mean subject to sudden mood changes. Trap: equable and placid are synonyms meaning calm, the opposite. Tyrannical fits on its own (players afraid to speak) but captures only the savage side, not the swings, and has no partner. Artistic is unrelated. Definitions: mercurial = unpredictably changeable; volatile = liable to change rapidly; equable = even-tempered. Lesson: when the clue shows two extremes, the answer describes the change between them, not one extreme.

questions.stem: A single undisclosed conflict of interest can _____ an otherwise rigorous study, since readers who learn of it will reasonably doubt every judgment the authors made.
questions.explain: Clue: "otherwise rigorous" and readers "will reasonably doubt every judgment" mean the study is damaged. Predict: weaken, spoil. Vitiate and undermine both mean impair the effectiveness of. Trap: bolster and buttress are synonyms meaning support, which would not cause doubt. Complicate fits on its own but is too mild for doubting "every judgment" and has no partner. Delay is unrelated. Definitions: vitiate = spoil, weaken, invalidate; buttress = support; bolster = strengthen. Lesson: "otherwise" signals that the blank opposes the positive description.

questions.stem: The court rebuked the plaintiff's attorneys for their _____ tactics, noting that they had requested eleven postponements in two years without offering a substantive reason for any of them.
questions.explain: Clue: "eleven postponements in two years." Predict: delaying. Dilatory (intended to cause delay) and delaying match. Trap: expeditious and prompt are synonyms meaning quick, the opposite. Aggressive fits on its own (a court might rebuke aggressive tactics) but has no partner and ignores postponements. Deceptive fits loosely (no real reasons) but has no partner. Definitions: dilatory = slow, tending to delay; expeditious = speedy and efficient. Lesson: the noting-clause is the definition; do not choose a word that merely fits "rebuked."

questions.stem: Although the witness had at first refused to commit herself, at the second hearing she _____ that she had seen the defendant at the warehouse that night.
questions.explain: Signal: "Although... refused to commit herself" means at the second hearing she did commit. Predict: stated firmly. Averred and asserted both mean declared positively. Trap: speculated and conjectured are synonyms meaning guessed; a guess is not commitment, so "although" loses its contrast. Remembered fits on its own but describes memory, not a firm statement, and has no partner. Averted is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: aver = state confidently; conjecture = guess; avert = turn away or prevent. Lesson: "although" demands a real contrast; check that the trap pair does not repeat the first clause.

questions.stem: Years of reporting from conflict zones had not, as her colleagues assumed, _____ her to suffering; if anything, each assignment left her more vulnerable to the images she carried home.
questions.explain: Signal: "had not... as assumed" plus "if anything... more vulnerable" means the assumed effect was toughening, and the reality was the opposite. Predict: accustomed, hardened. Inured and habituated both mean made used to. Trap: sensitized and attuned are synonyms describing what actually happened, so "had not" would contradict "if anything, more vulnerable." Reconciled fits on its own (accepting suffering) but means coming to accept, not becoming desensitized, and has no partner. Endeared does not fit. Definitions: inure = accustom to hardship; habituate = make used to. Lesson: "if anything" reverses the assumption; the blank names the assumption.

questions.stem: Unlike his _____ father, who had set aside a portion of every harvest against the inevitable drought years, the heir spent each year's income as soon as it arrived.
questions.explain: Clue: the father "set aside a portion of every harvest against... drought years." Signal: "Unlike" contrasts him with the spending heir. Predict: saving, planning ahead. Provident and thrifty match. Trap: improvident and spendthrift are synonyms describing the heir, not the father. Pious fits on its own but has no partner and has nothing to do with saving. Providential is the sounds-related trap: it means lucky or divinely arranged. Definitions: provident = providing for the future; improvident = not saving; providential = fortunate. Lesson: with "unlike," make sure you describe the right person.

questions.stem: The screenwriter's dialogue, though technically competent, relies so heavily on _____ phrases that audiences can often finish the characters' sentences before they do.
questions.explain: Clue: "audiences can often finish the characters' sentences" means the phrases are predictable. Predict: overused. Hackneyed and trite both mean worn out by overuse. Trap: novel and fresh are synonyms meaning new, the opposite; note that novel here is the adjective, not a book. Colloquial fits on its own (everyday speech) but means informal, not overused, and has no partner. Pithy (brief and forceful) is unsupported. Definitions: hackneyed = clichéd; trite = stale; colloquial = conversational. Lesson: predictability clues point to cliché words.

questions.stem: Contrary to the expectation that the long voyage would _____ the crew, the sailors arrived in port in better health than when they had departed, a fact the ship's surgeon attributed to his citrus rations.
questions.explain: Signal: "Contrary to the expectation" and "better health" mean the expected effect was weakening. Predict: weaken. Enervate and debilitate both mean drain of strength. Trap: invigorate and energize are synonyms describing what actually happened; energize is also the sounds-related trap, since enervate looks like energize but means the opposite. Demoralize fits on its own (long voyages can lower morale) but concerns spirit, not health, and has no partner. Acclimate (adjust) does not fit. Definitions: enervate = weaken; debilitate = make feeble. Lesson: enervate means weaken; never energize.

questions.stem: Critics of the decision argue that it was _____, made within hours of the first reports and before any of the agency's own analysts had reviewed the data.
questions.explain: Clue: "within hours" and "before any... analysts had reviewed the data." Predict: rushed. Precipitate (secondary sense, as an adjective: done suddenly without thought) and hasty match. Trap: measured and considered are synonyms meaning carefully thought out, the opposite. Unpopular fits on its own (critics oppose it) but has no partner and ignores the timing. Condensed is the sounds-related trap from chemistry, where a precipitate forms out of solution. Definitions: precipitate (adj.) = rash, sudden; considered = carefully thought about. Lesson: precipitate as an adjective means hasty.

questions.stem: Far from being the taciturn recluse of popular legend, the inventor was _____ to a fault, as likely to lecture a stranger on train schedules as on the principles of electromagnetism.
questions.explain: Signal: "Far from being the taciturn recluse" and the clue "lecture a stranger." Predict: talkative. Garrulous and loquacious both mean very talkative. Trap: reticent and reserved are synonyms that restate "taciturn," the legend rejected. Eccentric fits on its own (oddly lecturing on train schedules) but has no partner and does not mean talkative. Gracious fits "to a fault" grammatically but has no partner and ignores "taciturn." Definitions: garrulous = excessively talkative; loquacious = talkative; taciturn = silent; reticent = reluctant to speak. Lesson: "far from X" wants the opposite of X; here X is taciturn.

questions.stem: The headmaster could _____ occasional lateness, but he made it clear that he would not abide deliberate disrespect toward the teaching staff.
questions.explain: Signal: "could X... but would not abide" means X is a form of putting up with. Predict: tolerate. Countenance (secondary sense, as a verb: tolerate, approve) and condone match. Trap: forbid and prohibit are synonyms; "could forbid lateness but would not abide disrespect" destroys the contrast. Anticipate fits grammatically but has no partner and does not contrast with "would not abide." Face is the sounds-related trap for countenance as a noun (face). Definitions: countenance (verb) = tolerate; condone = accept, overlook; abide = tolerate. Lesson: countenance as a verb means permit.

questions.stem: The new imaging technique may _____ the need for exploratory surgery in many patients, allowing physicians to locate tumors that were previously detectable only on the operating table.
questions.explain: Clue: tumors "previously detectable only on the operating table" can now be located without surgery. Predict: remove. Obviate (remove the need for) and eliminate match. Trap: necessitate and entail are synonyms meaning require; the technique does not require surgery. Reduce fits on its own but means lessen, not remove, and has no partner; the "many patients" already limits the scope. Obscure is unrelated. Definitions: obviate = make unnecessary; necessitate = make necessary; entail = involve as a consequence. Lesson: obviate always attaches to a need or a problem and removes it.

questions.stem: _____ by the failure of their first expedition, the explorers planned the second with far greater care, doubling their provisions and hiring local guides.
questions.explain: Clue: failure led to "far greater care" and extra precautions. Predict: made humble, sobered. Chastened and humbled both mean made more restrained by experience. Trap: emboldened and heartened are synonyms meaning encouraged; failure does not encourage, and boldness would not produce greater care. Delayed fits the sentence on its own but has no partner and ignores the change in attitude. Chastised is the sounds-related trap: it means scolded, which requires a person doing the scolding. Definitions: chastened = subdued, corrected by hardship; chastised = rebuked. Lesson: chastened describes an inner change; chastised describes a scolding.

questions.stem: Fearful of alienating any constituency, the foundation's annual report had been revised into something wholly _____, so stripped of controversial claims that it said almost nothing at all.
questions.explain: Clue: "fearful of alienating" and "stripped of controversial claims." Predict: inoffensive. Anodyne (secondary sense: deliberately inoffensive) and innocuous match. Trap: inflammatory and provocative are synonyms meaning likely to offend, the opposite. Unreadable fits on its own but has no partner and says nothing about offense. Analgesic is the literal-sense trap: anodyne originally means a painkiller, but analgesic describes medicine, not a report. Definitions: anodyne = bland, not likely to offend; innocuous = harmless; analgesic = pain-relieving. Lesson: anodyne in prose means inoffensive and bland.

questions.stem: The coalition had always been _____, its member parties quarreling openly over everything from budget priorities to the seating plan at state dinners, so few observers were surprised when it finally collapsed.
questions.explain: Clue: "quarreling openly over everything." Predict: quarrelsome. Fractious and contentious both mean prone to quarrels. Trap: harmonious and concordant are synonyms meaning in agreement, the opposite. Fragile fits the sentence on its own (it collapsed) but has no partner and does not capture the quarreling. Fractional is the sounds-related trap. Definitions: fractious = unruly, quarrelsome; contentious = argumentative; concordant = agreeing. Lesson: when the clue gives a specific behavior (quarreling), choose the words that name that behavior, not its result (fragile).

questions.stem: Coined by a hostile reviewer to ridicule the painters, the label was at first _____, but within a decade the artists themselves had adopted it with evident pride.
questions.explain: Clue: "coined... to ridicule" by a "hostile reviewer"; "but... with evident pride" shows a later reversal. Predict: insulting. Pejorative and derogatory both mean expressing contempt. Trap: laudatory and complimentary are synonyms meaning praising, the later attitude, not the original one. Inaccurate is the misnomer trap: it fits on its own but has no partner, and nothing says the label was wrong, only that it was mocking. Obscure is unsupported. Definitions: pejorative = disparaging; laudatory = praising; misnomer = wrong name. Lesson: purpose words ("to ridicule") tell you the label's tone, not its accuracy.
